topic_summaries.UK Heatwave, Wildfires and Drought Crisi:
• The Guardian and Channel 4 News explicitly link the crisis to fossil fuels and climate change; GB News and The Sun take a more practical, less politicised tone — focusing on groundwater health and drought-tolerant gardening respectively
• BBC and Metro lead on the coming weather relief; The Independent and The Guardian emphasise the ongoing systemic failures — water company leaks, lack of reservoirs, and inadequate wildfire infrastructure
• The Guardian and The i scrutinise government policy most critically — questioning Burnham's climate ambition and the hosepipe ban's hypocrisy — while GB News and Evening Standard largely report his emergency measures at face value
topic_summaries.Global Extreme Weather and Climate Impac:
• The Guardian dominates coverage, framing extreme weather (heatwaves, wildfires, floods, drought) as an interconnected, ongoing climate emergency with human consequences across Europe, Asia, and the Global South
• The Independent offers more varied framing — reporting both on climate-driven European wildfires and a counter-narrative attributing Assam flooding to human error rather than climate change
• Daily Mail and GB News largely sidestep direct climate framing, with the Mail burying climate stories amid unrelated headlines and GB News leading with cautiously optimistic angles (reef recovery, British cocoa)
topic_summaries.North Sea Oil and Fossil Fuel Industry:
• Sky News focuses on UK industry lobbying pressure on the PM over North Sea approvals, though source text is inaccessible
• The Guardian frames fossil fuels as a global expansion problem — covering India's coal surge and AI's role in boosting fossil fuel productivity, emphasising negative climate consequences
• Both Guardian pieces share a critical, risk-focused framing; no outlet here offers a pro-industry or economic-benefit perspective
topic_summaries.Rosebank Oil Field Decision:
• Evening Standard and Channel 4 News focus on the procedural milestone of the consultation closing, with Channel 4 giving platform to a critical voice framing Rosebank as a "distraction"
• GB News emphasises political tension, highlighting Burnham's expected delay and internal Whitehall concerns about the "optics" of approving drilling amid heatwaves and wildfires
topic_summaries.Electric Vehicles and Net Zero Policy De:
• BBC and The Independent report factually on the ZEV mandate review, with The Independent notably highlighting polling showing public opposition to scaling back EV targets
• GB News frames the story through security and sovereignty concerns — emphasising China's "takeover" of London buses and industry "fury" at Labour — while also covering the Net Zero prison cost story under an EV/climate framing
• The Guardian and The i focus on climate accountability, with The Guardian criticising PM Burnham's approach and The i warning consumers of rising EV prices as a consequence of weakened targets
topic_summaries.Reform and Political Pushback on Climate:
• The Guardian and Sky News scrutinise Reform's climate scepticism critically — framing Tice's heatwave comments as misinformation — while GB News presents Reform's water and energy policies sympathetically, as practical solutions to real problems
• GB News consistently frames net zero and green policies as costly or counterproductive ("madness," "woke," "bribing Britons"); The Guardian counters with stories exposing fossil fuel interests undermining climate action (Alito, Trump/ESA, Arctic report)
• The Independent and The i offer more nuanced middle-ground takes, acknowledging climate progress while critiquing policy delivery failures like the £1bn wind farm curtailment costs
topic_summaries.Andy Burnham's Climate Leadership:
• Channel 4 News frames Burnham's climate position as uncertain and unresolved, highlighting public ambiguity around his stance
• The Guardian shifts focus away from individual politicians entirely, emphasising concrete policy solutions needed at a national level
• Contrasting approaches: Channel 4 centres on political figures and indecision; The Guardian on actionable climate responses

How many new reservoirs have been built in the UK over the same period? A. None. Nada. Zilch. 
In fact, not a single reservoir – vital for the prevention of water shortages and the management of river flows – has been built in the United Kingdom (total area: 94,000 square miles) since 1992. Meanwhile, since 2000, approximately 20 new, large dams or reservoirs have been built in Germany, and in France there are more than 100 water storage projects under construction. 
I use this litany of comparative statistics in case anyone is wondering why millions of households in the UK have hosepipe bans in force. The management of one of the nation’s most precious assets has simply not been a priority for more than three decades, which roughly coincides with the time that our water supply has been privatised, and the requirement to pay dividends to shareholders took precedence over the need to provide a reliable supply of water to customers.

 
In March last year, Clive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South and a vigorous campaigner against water privatisation, presented to Parliament the most damning comparison of all. “In the 35 years before privatisation, almost 100 reservoirs were built,” he said. “In the 35 years since privatisation, not one major English reservoir has been built.” 
And so, today, 10 of our water companies, covering huge swathes of land from East Anglia to West Wales, have hosepipe bans in force, requiring us to let our plants die and our lawns go brown in response to what we are told is an ongoing “crisis”, but is actually a situation that has been entirely foreseeable for the past 20 years or more. We haven’t suddenly run out of water: we lack the infrastructure needed to capture, store, transport and conserve it. 
Clearly, the rolling heatwaves have exacerbated the problem, and, by any measure, the weather this summer has been extreme. But, it’s not as if climate change has suddenly come upon us. No, what has caused the current emergency is not a few weeks of sunshine and heat, but more than 30 years of neglect and underinvestment. So, here’s another statistic to chew on: since they were privatised, Britain’s water companies have paid between £72bn and £85bn to shareholders. The heatwave is an easy excuse for the shortfall in our water supply. 
Most winters, rain falls in the UK to such an extent that our reservoirs are overflowing. But no one has thought it worth building new ones to save for that sunny day. People walk through Hampstead Heath, where the grass has turned yellow-brown due to a lack of rain (AFP/Getty)


Wessex Water has introduced a hosepipe ban for 1.4 million customers across the South West, marking its first restriction in 50 years and taking the total number of people affected in England to over 27 million.

articles.jina_text:
Some areas will have the ‘first meaningful rain for a long time’ this week, the Met Office said, after weeks of heatwaves and dry weather.

        







Much of the UK is experiencing drought after a dry, hot summer (Yui Mok/PA)
PA Wire



Rebecca Speare-Cole
5 minutes ago







A new hosepipe ban has come into force as forecasters warned parts of the UK could be hit by flooding, with rain set finally to hit drought-stricken land.




Some areas in the country will have the “first meaningful rain for a long time” in the coming days, the Met Office said, after weeks of heatwaves and dry weather have left many areas facing water shortages.








On Tuesday, a hosepipe ban begins for all of Wessex Water’s 1.4 million customers across areas in Bath, Somerset, Dorset and Wiltshire.




It is the first ban the company has put in place for 50 years, since the summer of 1976.




Announcing the temporary restriction, the company cited increased demand during the dry weather but also longer-term weather forecasts that mean resources must be protected for customers and the environment.




More than 27 million people across England have now had hosepipe use restricted in their area.




Following the fifth heatwave of the summer, this week is forecast to be wetter with cooler conditions that are much closer to average for the time of year, the Met Office said.


(PA Graphics)
PA Graphics




Showers are expected on Tuesday in the north of the country, particularly in the North West, and another area of rain will move into the South West by the evening, the Met Office’s deputy chief forecaster Mike Silverstone said.




This will then likely spread east across the South, bringing the first spell of widespread rain to areas in need the most, he added.


Parts of the UK are forecast to see heavy rain this week (Jordan Pettitt/PA)
PA Wire




“Thursday will be a day of heavy showers across much of the UK, while some of these will be heavy some areas will miss them altogether,” Mr Silverstone said.











“As some of these showers could be intense, there is a chance of some surface water flooding as the rain falls on very dry and hard ground.”




By Friday, the conditions are expected to turn drier once again through the weekend before more rain is forecast next week.









The change comes after the UK’s fifth heatwave of the summer, during which the hottest day of the year was recorded in Kew Gardens, London, on Thursday when temperatures reached 38.1C.


Fires have burned across the country following the hot and dry weather (Jacob King/PA)
PA Wire




The forecast rain may bring some welcome relief to parched land and fire-fighters tackling wildfires.

articles.title: Solar panel critic now 'supporter of plan'
articles.raw_rss: A dispute over a solar panel plan is resolved, with the complainant now a proponent for the site.
articles.raw_meta: A dispute over a solar panel plan is resolved, with the complainant now a proponent for the site.
articles.jina_text:
A critic of a proposed solar panel site in Guernsey says he is now a "complete supporter of the plan" after going through the details with the applicant.
Applicant Len Shephard said his proposals for 72 panels on a site behind his house in St Sampson could power five Guernsey households and save 505 trees a year.
The application initially received a complaint from Chris Chadwick, due to the site being defined as a greenfield area. However, Shephard and Chadwick have since met to go through the applications details, and Chadwick said he had been won over.
Planning officials are still considering the application.


Chadwick said that the plan has had "a lot of thought put into it"
Shepard said Chadwick became a supporter after he was "able to show him all of the information".
"He was good enough to just say: 'Well, it's nothing like I thought in the first place.' 
"The information is available to a degree on the planning website but there was no substitute for sitting down like this."














He added the panels would be "fully demountable" and in the future "someone can just take it apart and you'd never know it was there".
Shephard said the site was "used for greenhousing" and had sat for "45 years doing nothing" due to buried greenhouse materials beneath the field.
He said: "It's designated as greenfield because there's no choice for the planning. It's either horticulture or agriculture. 
"So we're kind of stuck with that... you're not going to be able to do any farming on it."
He added that proposals to build on greenfield sites should "be looked at on a case-by-case basis".







More news stories for Guernsey





Listen to the latest news for Guernsey
Chadwick explained his initial complaint was due to "little detail" being available online about the application.
He said: "It just said 72 panels and my initial reaction was that's going to cover all of the area.





"I saw the planning application right at the end of its period of notification so, by the time I looked at the website, the data wasn't there."
After learning more, Chadwick said Shephard "has put a lot of thought into making this work as best as possible."
Chadwick said he is now a "complete supporter of the of the plan" because Shephard had "considered all of the things that I asked questions about".
He said that "the panels are being stood up off the ground" so that grass and wildlife has access to the sun.
Chadwick added: "He probably won't see financial return from it his lifetime, so it's not a commercial decision: it's an altruistic decision to actually do the right thing."
The application has just seen a site assessment undertaken, according to the States' planning website.

Burnham is choosing jobs over climate security. That’s a big risk

Gaby Hinsliff






The PM’s net zero pragmatism may please some voters, but as parts of the country go up in flames, it’s an increasingly hard sell





When the siren sounded on Friday night, my first thought was fire.
Weeks of unrelenting sun in the normally soggy Peak District, where I was visiting my mum, have bleached green valleys a dangerously dry, crispy blond. One of her neighbours had earlier pointed out an ominous cloud of smoke on the horizon, coming from one of the wildfires raging all summer on the moor. When that harsh, discordant shriek blared from every mobile phone in the house, I was half-braced for an evacuation order, not what turned out to be a faintly melodramatic warning to the nation to lay off the barbecues. A false alarm, of sorts, but one that felt uneasily like a wake-up call.

Scientists can warn until they’re blue in the face about the consequences of what we’re doing to the planet, but nothing beats the visceral shock of idly scrolling on your phone and seeing panicky footage of flames leaping over suburban British fences, or terrified horses being turned loose from fields where the hedges are starting to catch light. A friend just back from the south of France, somewhere far enough from the raging wildfires there to be considered safe, was spooked by ash raining from the sky as she ate lunch in the garden: it felt like the beginning of an apocalypse, she said, or the opening scenes of a disaster movie. Something has shifted even in people who were once blase about the climate crisis, and judging by last week’s sudden flurry of government activity – a Cobra meeting on fighting wildfires called after hefty pressure from the Greens, extra support for drought-stricken farmers, and finally that emergency alert lighting up everyone’s phones – Andy Burnham has clocked the dangers of not being seen to respond.


Yet there’s something jarring about a new prime minister spending the hottest summer on record talking up the prospect of new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea, or consulting on easing net zero targets for carmakers. He was rightly quick to visit people affected by a wildfire near the West Midlands town of Stourbridge, but has been noticeably slower to respond publicly to warnings from the town’s Labour MP, Cat Eccles, that this is not the time to start extracting yet more fossil fuels. So far, his is more a strategy for picking up the pieces of damage already done than for gripping the root causes.

articles.jina_text:
The village of Faka in Sinjar was overrun by Islamic State in 2014 and retaken in 2017. All photographs: Chris Huby/Le Pictorium




Nearly a decade after fighting ended in northern Iraq, the climate crisis has brought extreme heat and a water shortage, making life almost impossible

By Chris Huby, in Sinjar




The first thing that strikes visitors arriving in Faka, a small village in Sinjar district, northern Iraq, is the silence. No children play in the streets. No shops are open. Roofless houses stretch across the hillside, their walls pockmarked by shellfire, while weeds and wild grasses grow through collapsed living rooms.
A decade after Islamic State (IS) swept across the region, war remains visible everywhere. But according to the people who returned, another enemy has quietly taken its place.



View image in fullscreen

 
 
Rajab Mohammed says the problem in his village of Faka is no longer Islamic State but water and jobs 
“Today, the problem isn’t only IS,” says Rajab Mohammed, 62, the village’s mukhtar, standing above the ruins of Faka. “It’s water. It’s jobs. It’s the future.”
Across Sinjar, abandoned houses now outnumber occupied ones. The battle against IS has ended. The battle to save the villages against drought and neglect has only just begun, and time is not on its side.
Before August 2014, about 150 families lived in Faka. When IS fighters seized the Sinjar region, residents fled as frontlines advanced across north-western Iraq. In August 2014, IS launched what the UN has recognised as a genocide against the ethnic minority Yazidi community. Thousands were killed and more than 6,000 people, mostly women and children, were abducted.

Rivers in the Sinjar region have dried up as rainfall has become more erratic and temperatures have risen 
While Faka and the nearby village of Qubq escaped the mass killings that devastated other nearby villages, coalition airstrikes and ground fighting left much of the area destroyed. Today, only about 20 families have returned. The rest have settled elsewhere, discouraged by the lack of reconstruction, jobs and basic services in a region where the climate crisis is making rural livelihoods such as farming increasingly precarious.
“People ask why families don’t come back. The answer is simple. Where would they live? How would they earn a living?” says Aqil Ridha from Qubq.

articles.raw_rss: Heavy showers are expected over the next few days, bringing a risk of flash flooding.  But there are early indications heatwave conditions could return in September.

articles.jina_text:
Although heavy showers are expected for many, the places across England and Wales most in need of significant rain may not see much of it in the coming days.
Most of the showers will fall across parts of north-west England, Northern Ireland and southern Scotland, with some parts of south-east England staying dry.
Where the heaviest showers do fall, there is a risk of hail, lightning and the potential for flash flooding.



Where will it rain?




Tuesday will start wet across many northern and central parts of the UK. Scotland and Northern Ireland will stay showery through much of the day, with some longer spells of rain across northeast Scotland and the Northern Isles. 
Further south, a cold front will bring cloud and some spots of light rain to parts of southern England and Wales early on, though some areas may stay entirely dry.
By Wednesday, an area of low pressure will bring sunny spells and frequent showers across north-west England, Northern Ireland and southern Scotland. 
Some of these showers will become heavy and thundery but south-east England will stay largely dry.
On Thursday, the showers will become more widespread as low pressure drifts southwards across the UK. 




Image source, BBC Weather
Image caption, 

Widespread showers and thunderstorms will affect some areas of the UK that have not seen significant rain for a period of days with the potential to cause flash flooding




Thunderstorms are expected to develop more widely, though some of the areas which need the rain most may avoid them altogether.
Some of the showers on Thursday will be very heavy and slow-moving, with the risk of hail, lightning and localised flooding.



Why do summer storms lead to flash flooding?




Drought officials have declared 71.3% of England is now in drought, after the nation recorded its driest July since records began in 1836. All of Wales is also in drought.
During periods of drought, ground can become very hard and compacted, which can make it more water repellent and increase run off.





Image caption, 

England is currently experiencing a flash drought according to the National Drought Group, brought about by a combination of very low rainfall and higher temperatures




Downpours from intense summer thunderstorms can fall faster than the water can soak into the ground and, instead, it rushes over the surface, leading to flash flooding.
Heavy summer thunderstorms don't mean an end to a drought, as rivers, groundwater levels and reservoirs can still be depleted for months.






Why drought can lead to dangerous flooding





15 August 2022



Arctic air moves in




As well as turning more unsettled in the coming days, the area of low pressure which is bringing the showers will also shepherd in some much cooler air from the Arctic.
Temperatures for most will drop below average for the first time in weeks. 
Scotland and Northern Ireland can expect highs of 13-18C.

Reform’s deputy leader has been accused of spreading misinformation after he dismissed efforts to tackle the climate crisis and urged British people to enjoy the warmth of the recent heatwaves.
Richard Tice prompted a backlash from nurses, medical experts and green campaigners on Monday after he told a press conference he believed it was “arrogant” to try to stop the climate emergency, while encouraging people to focus on upsides such as better English wine.

Asked about the recent extreme heat, Tice told a press conference: “Of course, the climate changes, but where is the evidence that net zero is going to stop it? Where is the evidence? There is no evidence.
“Climate change has always happened. It always will. Maybe the smarter thing to do is to adapt to it than think arrogantly that you can stop it.”


He added: “When it’s a bit warm, let’s enjoy it. And if it means that English wine and sparkling wine gets better and better, fantastic. That means we can take on the French – fantastic. Let’s celebrate some of these things rather than just be sort of doom and gloom about it.”
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “Richard Tice’s comments are tone-deaf. With wildfires raging across the UK and drought threatening water supplies and food security, comments like these don’t just raise serious questions about his judgment – they also expose where his interests really lie.”
Tice’s comments came amid a record-breaking summer during which temperatures have risen above 35C several times, causing thousands of deaths, millions of hospital visits and costing the UK an estimated £4bn in economic output.







‘I couldn’t breathe’: the deadly health burden of wildfire smoke

Read more
The government has estimated that 2,877 people died as a result of high temperatures during the May and June heatwaves – double the figure for the whole of last summer.
The climate breakdown has been linked to the increasing frequency of wildfires, which are burning larger areas across many parts of the world. The so-called firewave the UK witnessed weeks ago was the most widespread the country has seen, with the combination of wet winters and prolonged heatwaves exacerbating the risk.


New figures published in the Lancet on Tuesday reveal older people are affected by the heat at lower temperatures than previously thought, while medical professionals say they are struggling to deal with the surge in patients.
A spokesperson for the Royal College of Nursing said: “Those calling for people to enjoy the impacts of climate change should say it to the nurses collapsing in hospitals where temperatures are hitting 36 degrees.
“Or to the thousands of patients lining corridors every day as extreme heat causes severe illness among the vulnerable, older people and even those without pre-existing conditions.

articles.title: Rosebank oil field a ‘distraction’ from real climate problems – Electrify Britain CEO
articles.raw_rss: Andy Burnham now has to decide whether to approve a controversial North Atlantic oil drilling plan - after a consultation on the proposal came to an end.
articles.raw_content:
Andy Burnham now has to decide whether to approve a controversial North Atlantic oil drilling plan – after a consultation on the proposal came to an end.
The £8.7 billion Rosebank project, located around 80 miles north-west of the Shetland Islands is seeking approval, alongside the Jackdaw gas field off Aberdeen.
Production at both sites was given the go-ahead under Rishi Sunak’s government, but a legal challenge by Greenpeace put those plans on hold.
Industry bodies say the sites will provide jobs and improve the UK’s energy security but opponents claim that extracting fossil fuels from the UK’s largest undeveloped oil field could have serious implications for the climate. While more than 200 musicians, including Brian Eno and Thom Yorke, have written to the Prime Minister urging him to reject the plans.
To discuss this further we spoke to climate researcher Dr Pancho Lewis, assistant professor at Durham University, and Camilla Born who was an advisor to COP 26 President Alok Sharma.

European farmers face ‘unprecedented crisis’ after successive heatwaves


Vegetable and grain growers call for urgent action, warning of ‘catastrophic’ harvests due to continent-wide drought




Successive intense heatwaves and an increasingly severe, continent-wide drought have left many of Europe’s farmers in an “unprecedented” crisis, with vegetable and grain growers in particular warning of “catastrophic” harvests.
French vegetable production is down by “a very significant extent” compared with previous years, French growers have said, with shortfalls put at 25% for courgettes, 35% for lettuces, 40% for peas, 60% for broccoli and 50% to 100% for artichokes.

“The vegetable sector is facing a historic crisis,” said Prince de Bretagne, which groups together more than 1,300 vegetable producers in Brittany, calling for “urgent action” to address a “dramatic” fall in yields and in the quality of many crops.


Accelerated, human-caused global heating and a supersized El Niño have scorched fields across Europe this summer, with plant development prevented by temperatures routinely exceeding 30C and often 35C, almost no rainfall, and hot winds.
“Usually one region fares better, which helps compensate,” Eric Legras, of the 4,400-member French canned and frozen vegetable producers’ association, told Le Monde. “This year, all our main production areas have been hit, and at the same time.”
Cereal production has been equally hard hit, with the agriculture ministry estimating the maize harvest in France – Europe’s largest grains producer – will be down by 35% on 2025 levels at about 9m tonnes, a quantity last seen in 1980.
Part of the fall is due to farmers’ switching to other crops, such as sunflowers, the ministry said, but it also reflects the impact of this summer’s vicious heatwaves, which have battered the crucial crop during critical stages of its growth cycle.
That is likely to cause big problems for livestock farmers. With dairy cows typically starting to suffer from heat stress above 25C, many producers have already reported milk yields down by 10%-15%. Most are now also concerned about winter feed.

articles.title: China’s leftover renewable energy could power UK for more than a year
articles.raw_rss: In just six months, China was forced to turn away clean solar power equivalent to annual energy demand of Mexico
articles.raw_meta: In just six months, China was forced to turn away clean solar power equivalent to annual energy demand of Mexico
articles.jina_text:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
Jump to content


























Swipe for next article










China lost a quarter of the wind and solar power it generated in the first half of this year because its grid had no room for it, wasting enough electricity to run the United Kingdom or Mexico for more than a year.
The country turned away 360 terawatt hours (TWh) between January and June, 49 per cent more than the same period last year, according to a report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air and Global Energy Monitor. 
Had that power been used, it would have covered the entire growth in Chinese electricity demand over the six months and allowed coal generation to fall. Instead, China’s coal generation rose 3.4 per cent year on year, reversing a decline that was the first in a decade.





The practice of rejecting electricity is known as curtailment, and it means switching off wind turbines and solar farms, or refusing to accept what they generate, because the network has no room for the electricity at that moment. 
Electricity cannot be held on a wire, so power that is not used as it is produced is lost, and the fossil fuel plants that could have been displaced keep running.

At the root of it is a coal building programme that has continued despite orders to rein it in, researchers said. 


China brought 30 gigawatts (GW) of new coal-fired capacity into operation in the first half of the year, the most in any first half for a decade and 43 per cent more than last year, while retiring only 2.7GW. Another 25.4GW began construction, and 274GW are in the pipeline, equivalent to 22 per cent of the coal fleet already running.
This has resulted in a system with more generating capacity than it can use. Coal plants are running fewer hours, yet long-term contracts still guarantee them a share of demand, with coal generators expected to sign annual contracts this year covering 60 to 70 per cent of the electricity they delivered the year before. That reserves space on the grid regardless of how much cheaper clean power is available.



"China's coal buildout is a warning about overcapacity, not a blueprint for energy security," said Qi Qin, China analyst at the research centre. "Coal capacity is still growing because of legacy approvals and policy protections, even as plants run fewer hours and large volumes of clean electricity go unused."

Transmission is the other constraint. Lines have not been built fast enough to move electricity from the deserts and grasslands of the north and west, where China has built its largest solar and wind farms, to the industrial cities of the east that consume it.

Another heatwave could be on the horizon, the Met Office has predicted, as the UK reels from a month of unprecedented hot and dry conditions.
Temperatures are expected to finally come down this week after the fifth heatwave brought the hottest day of the year so far, with provisional peaks of 38.1C. 
But the Met Office has warned there is a chance of a late-season heatwave developing in the south as the UK moves into the meteorological autumn.





According to the forecaster’s long-term forecast for 30 August to 13 September, “there is a chance that late-season hot spells or heatwaves develop, especially in the south.” 





open image in gallery
The UK has seen five heatwaves so far this year (Getty)
The Met Office predicts “drier, more settled weather is slightly more likely towards the south and east. Temperatures are again likely to be near to or above average overall”.

It comes as almost three-quarters of England, and all of Wales, has been plunged into drought after the driest July on record. 


By 15 July this year, the UK had already recorded more days above 30C than in the whole of 1976, which was known for its long-lasting heatwave.
Prime minister Andy Burnham warned just last week that Britain is a “tinderbox” as he visited Stourbridge in the West Midlands, where firefighters have been tackling wildfires.



West Midlands Fire Service declared a major incident on Thursday as a wildfire spread across more than 500 acres and destroyed 19 homes in the market town, one of several blazes to ravage the UK this week.





open image in gallery
The army has been called in to support wildfires (Getty)
Meanwhile, crews are continuing to fight several wildfires in South Wales on Monday after emergency services warned that risk remains high for this week.





On Friday evening, millions of people in England and Wales received an alert on their mobile devices warning them of a “very high risk of wildfires nationally”.
A temporary ban on disposable barbecues was put in place as the prime minister warned earlier this week that they may have caused some of the wildfires.
“I can’t, on this call today, say to you that all of them are down to disposable barbecues – they’re not, and I wouldn’t claim that,” he told BBC Radio 5 Live. “But it’s probable that some of them have been caused in that way.”

Met Office five day forecast

Today
Remaining cloudy in the north with outbreaks of rain, becoming heavier and more persistent across Northern Ireland and western Scotland during the afternoon. Further south, hazy sunshine will develop, making it feel very warm and humid.

Tonight
Outbreaks of rain across the north will spread into northern England and North Wales by dawn. Further south, it will remain dry with clear spells. A slight cooler night.

Britain will experience a spell of cooler and wetter conditions following its fifth heatwave of the year.

After several weeks of hot, dry weather, this week could see the return of rain and even some thunderstorms in parts of southern England.

A yellow heat health alert remains in place until 9am on Tuesday for London, the South East and South West.

However forecasters predict this week will bring the most ‘changeable’ conditions since the end of June.

Spotlight on UN desertification summit as it mulls how to spend $12bn war chest


Extreme weather has raised the significance of Cop17 talks starting this week on tackling drought and land degradation




As swathes of the northern hemisphere bake in what could be the hottest year on record, with wildfires blazing across North America and Europe and heatwaves afflicting millions across Asia, the UN’s bi-annual talks on desertification have assumed much greater importance – and have started attracting more money.
Work will begin this week on allocating more than $12bn (£8.9bn) to vulnerable countries to help them deal with drought and land degradation, when scores of countries gather in Mongolia for Cop17.

Yasmine Fouad, executive secretary of the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), whose 17th “conference of the parties” begins in Ulaanbaatar on 17 August, said the negotiations would “send a positive signal of multilateralism”.


The key aim is to put pledges of billions of dollars made two years ago into action through projects in the developing world.
Countries around the world are bracing for food price rises as a result of damage to harvests from record heat and lack of water, and the World Food Programme predicts that 50 million more people could be pushed into hunger by the “super El Niño” weather system currently developing. Initiatives to restore land and prevent drought have up to now been poorly funded and badly managed.
According to Fouad, that situation was changing rapidly as nations began to recognise the risk. “At the heart of our discussion is the topic of food security,” she said. “The more you work on restoring land, the more you have productive soil to ensure food security. That kind of narrative should be part of our finance [initiatives].”
The UNCCD was signed in 1992, one of a trio of environmental treaties launched at the Earth summit in Rio de Janeiro, alongside the better known UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), which is parent treaty to the Paris agreement of 2015; and the Convention on Biological Diversity, which includes targets on protecting species. Over the last three decades, the desertification treaty has been the “poor relation”, garnering the least attention of the three and producing scant progress.


But that is changing. Saudi Arabia – a petrostate that for years has blocked action on greenhouse gas emissions and any mention of fossil fuels at UNFCCC meetings, and has refused calls to provide climate finance – is an enthusiastic backer of UNCCD. Coping with 54C heat: Delhi slum diaries detail living in extreme temperatures


With heatwaves now recognised as disasters, personal testimonies are key to a new project that looks to protect those living in the most cramped districts of India’s capital




Every summer evening, Gulshan follows the same routine. She washes the floor of her one-room home several times so it cools a little for her four children to sleep on. Last summer, the family saved enough to buy a desert cooler, which uses evaporation as a cheaper alternative to air conditioning.
The family uses the appliance cautiously to save on energy costs. But even when it is on, Gulshan, who does not use a surname, has to dampeneveryone’s clothes before sleeping. The 39-year-old and her children now have rashes and one has a skin infection from the wet cloth against their skin.



View image in fullscreen
Gulshan writes in her heat diary. Photograph: Suchitra
This summer, Gulshan started jotting down these coping strategies in a garmi khata, or heat registry. “I feel relieved that at least somebody might read my family’s experiences,” she says.
They are one of 40 households in Sunder Nagri, a slum in north-east Delhi, documenting their experiences of surviving the city’s increasingly longer and more frequent heatwaves.
Over the last few years, cities across India have begun drawing up heat action plans – agreements formulated by a municipality or district administration on how to prepare for and respond to extreme heat.
While some incorporate data such as satellite-derived land surface temperatures to identify heat hotspots, there are still significant gaps in information on people, making it difficult to understand how heat is experienced differently across communities.
Aravind Unni, an urban planner and researcher in Delhi, says: “Experiences of heat are vastly different depending on geography, income, occupation, gender, caste, class.
“While we have some meteorological data on heat, what’s absolutely missing is people, community – what they feel, what they experience.”

A thermal image of Sunder Nagri’s main market area, showing a ground temperature of 54.1C (129.4F). Photograph: Sabique Ahmed/Greenpeace
Most data collated in heat planning is usually just meteorological, such as air temperatures and heatwave thresholds.. The idea for the heat diaries was to “move beyond just the numbers”, says Nibedita Saha, a Greenpeace India researcher who worked on the project.

articles.jina_text:
Wisley in Surrey has notched up 60 days with no recorded rainfall. Significant rain has been lacking elsewhere with most areas of England and Wales in drought.
There is some welcome rain forecast this week, though it's not likely to be significant or bring any change to the dry conditions.
It will also turn noticeably cooler in the coming days with temperatures falling below average across the UK.





Image caption, 

Rainfall accumulation over the next five days shows a chance of some rainfall for most of the UK, though no significant amount in southern England




High pressure has been dominant this summer leading to hot and dry weather, particularly across England and Wales.
There's been no significant rain in southern England for around two months which has led water levels in our rivers and reservoirs to drop significantly. All of Wales and most of England are in drought.
However, through this week high pressure will be replaced by the influence of low pressure and more unsettled conditions.
Some light rain is likely on Monday, mostly across northern areas of the UK.
Into Tuesday and Wednesday this will turn heavier and start to move into southern England.
While rain is therefore finally going to fall across the south, it may become more showery. This means the exact location and distribution of rainfall is still uncertain.
And while of course any rain will be welcome, it won't bring much improvement to conditions.
It will take weeks of above average rainfall into the autumn to make any significant changes to the drought.
However, it is likely to make a big difference to the emergency services who have been battling against the extreme weather and wildfires over the last few weeks.
The fire severity index - how severe a fire could be, should one start - will come down to low or moderate, according to forecasts from Natural England and the Met Office.






How much rain will end the drought?





6 August


Fires prompt national alert as 19 homes destroyed





2 days ago





Image caption, 

Temperatures will fall below average - indicated by the blue hue on map above - through this week



Turning much cooler




On Saturday the temperature peaked at 30.6C in southern England, making it the 40th day somewhere in the UK over 30C this year.
It's looking unlikely temperatures will peak this high again for the rest of the summer, which meteorologically ends on 31 August.
Temperatures on Monday and Tuesday will still be above average across England and Wales with highs of 20 to 26C.
But they will drop during the rest of the week as a mostly northerly airflow starts to have more influence.
By the end of the week, temperatures across the UK will be around 2 to 4C below average. Something we haven't seen much - if really at all - this summer.
Across Scotland and Northern Ireland temperatures will be around 14-17C and for England and Wales, 17-21C.
Nights will become much cooler, and in some part, even colder, too.

articles.jina_text:
Wildlife groups in Florida are celebrating record numbers of sea turtle nests this season, but experts warn Donald Trump’s recent gutting of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) could reverse decades of their recovery from the edge of extinction.
With more than two months of the summer nesting season still to run, loggerhead turtles have already made 13,770 nests, hundreds more than recorded in any previous year, along an 8.5-mile stretch of shoreline monitored by the Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach, on Florida’s Atlantic coast.

The same record has fallen on Sanibel island, on the Gulf coast, where loggerheads have laid 922 nests so far this year, surpassing the 2023 total of 878, according to the Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation.
The numbers reflect the ongoing revival of sea turtles since the 1970s, when overhunting, poaching and habitat loss pushed several species to the brink, including the loss of about 95% of the Caribbean’s population of green turtles.


View image in fullscreen
A sea turtle is prepared for a CT scan at the Loggerhead Marinelife Center. Photograph: Loggerhead Marinelife Center
The ESA, passed in 1973, enshrined protections that are paying dividends now because sea turtle hatchlings take years to decades to reach reproductive age. The loss of those safeguards, from Trump’s “death sentence” repeal last month of sections of the law to favor oil drilling, mining, logging and development interests, has some experts fearful that the recovery might have reached the high-water mark.


An alliance of environmental and wildlife groups is suing the Trump administration in part over a rule giving outsized deference to “economic considerations” when determining protections for endangered species and critical habitat.
“What we’re seeing is the result of several decades of sustained protection of these species under the ESA and various other measures to protect their habitat in different ways,” said David Godfrey, executive director of the Sea Turtle Conservancy, an advocacy group that is not a plaintiff in the lawsuit, but is supportive of it.
“It takes just about any species of sea turtle 20, 30 years to reach maturity, to come back and nest, to return to beaches where they were first protected as eggs or as hatchlings and afforded the opportunity to live without ending up in a fisherman’s net and on a table in a nice restaurant.
“So the recovery’s going on largely due to the ESA, which is one of the reasons why we’re all very concerned about the setbacks to the legislation.”
The ESA is credited with safeguarding more than 1,700 species and their habitats, preventing 99% of those listed from going extinct.
Godfrey said: “The detractors of the ESA sometimes say, ‘Oh, this thing is a failure. Look at all these animals that are still on the list. We haven’t removed a lot from the list.’ And I come right back and say, yeah, but look at all these animals that are on the list that we haven’t lost.

Nurses collapsing, builders with heatstroke, bus drivers in cabs that reach 44C. The new PM wanted to spend the summer talking about the cost of living – he should change his plans





I don’t think I have ever written before about a British strike directly related to the climate emergency. But that’s exactly what began late last week in north London, with a zeitgeisty connection to Andy Burnham’s fixation on buses: picket lines outside depots and massed walkouts, while the temperatures in the relevant parts of the capital and its suburbs hovered at about 34C (93F).
Last Friday, more than 1,500 drivers employed by the transport giant Arriva began a planned run of 26 stoppages through to October, affecting bus routes spread between London and Essex. Everything is being led by the union Unite, whose recent grievances include alleged company union-busting and assaults by the public on staff. But the fundamental basis of the dispute is at the heart of the national condition: the near-impossibility for millions of people of working through another insanely hot summer.



Most of Arriva North London’s buses, says Unite, have old-fashioned air cooling systems rather than air conditioning, which means that onboard temperatures have come down by only two or three degrees during this year’s five heatwaves. On other such vehicles, it insists, the air-con is broken. The cabs where drivers sit are essentially compact greenhouses, and can easily reach 40C or higher. And there is another grim twist: union members complain of a shortage of toilets on too many routes, meaning they refrain from drinking water. Unite has been warning about all this since the phases of intense heat that began back in May; its members, the union says, have experienced “heat exhaustion, heatstroke and dehydration”.
Arriva’s last financial figures showed a pre-tax profit of £133m. The company insists that it has “introduced short-term measures to protect drivers”, and is now also spending money on “longer-term fixes, including cab air-conditioning upgrades and our ongoing investment in new fleet”. But the root of its current problems seem clear. There is a longstanding failure, which runs across the UK’s public and private sectors – and also transcends national boundaries – to understand the mounting everyday effects of global heating, and to engage in what so many 21st-century companies and institutions remain so bad at: protective investment, with both eyes fixed not just on the searing inevitabilities of the future, but realities that are already here.


Arriva places tight restrictions on its drivers talking to the media, so Unite pointed me instead to Mo, who has worked for another London bus operator for over 15 years, and had come to a picket line to show the strikers his support. “When it’s very hot, it’s very difficult to concentrate,” he told me. “Imagine the heat you feel when you put your hand near an oven. As wildfires rage across Europe and Britain swelters through its hottest summer on record, literary fiction has a vital role to play in capturing the severe consequences of climate crisis




Earlier this summer, I travelled through Europe on a book tour. Everywhere I went, the heat broke records. In Italy, Germany and Spain, I sought refuge from the afternoon sun in air-conditioned hotels. In normally temperate Zurich, it averaged 37 degrees. I jumped into the Limmat for relief. On my final day in Warsaw, Poland had never been hotter – one of 14 countries to hit a historic high. In June, when I left to return to the US, Europe was scorching. At the end of July, as I write this, it is burning.
Since the heatwaves began, there have been more than 10,000 excess deaths. Yet for many, myself included, the high temperatures brought nothing more than inconvenience – uncomfortable commutes, heat rash, less time outdoors. This seems to be a defining feature of today’s climate crisis; deadly for some, banal for others. Even when the world is on fire, it somehow doesn’t feel like an emergency for everyone.

This disparity cast my mind back to Hurricane Sandy in 2012. I was living in New York, one of millions ordered to shelter in place. (I was lucky – hundreds of thousands were ordered to evacuate their homes.) I followed instructions. I stayed in my warm, dry apartment on the Upper West Side, watching trees swaying violently against the dark sky. The next morning, the rain had stopped; the sun was out, the air was still again and the power was still on. When I went outside to survey the damage, there was little to see except a few broken branches. The mood in my neighbourhood was jovial. The subways were closed, schools were shut, work was called off. Brunch was on.
In other parts of the city, it was a different story. Whole fleets of taxi cabs submerged in water, their canary yellow roofs peeking out; a huge midtown crane snapped cleanly in half; the collapsed wall of an apartment building. I watched and rewatched a video of a power plant exploding. Half a million people, including most of the residents of lower Manhattan, were now without electricity. The American news outlets focused almost exclusively on New York. The international news sites told a more complete story: Sandy killed 233 people in eight countries and caused $70bn in damage.
Several days after the storm, I volunteered in Chinatown, distributing basic goods – batteries, canned food and bottled water – to elderly people who lived on the highest floors of public housing buildings and hadn’t yet ventured outside since the storm. (the lifts weren’t working and they weren’t able to take the stairs). The apartments smelled of rotting food and unflushed toilets. The national guard rolled through the streets in tanks; rats brazenly stalked the pavements and Red Cross workers posed for photographs with locals. Two decades ago, economist Sir Nicholas Stern was asked by then chancellor Gordon Brown to carry out a review on the economics of climate change. The 700-page document that he produced would become a landmark shift in how climate change is framed: that it is an economic issue, and not just an environmental issue; that the cost of inaction is far greater than the cost of action; and that climate change is "the greatest market failure the world has seen". 
The Stern Review would go on to shape UK and EU climate policy for decades, helping to mainstream key decarbonisation tools such as carbon pricing and green investment. The years since have seen the price of green technologies plummet and major achievements like the 2015 Paris Agreement, which has given the world a framework for decarbonisation. But there has also been another, less positive story: of emissions continuing to rise year-on-year, and of extreme weather resulting from the climate crisis shifting from a future problem to a present emergency.
Given this contradictory context, how does Lord Stern view his own assessment, two decades on?
“Well, at the time we were accused of being alarmist, but in fact we understated the risks,” he tells The Independent, speaking over Zoom this week. “Every time a major new scientific report has come out, the climate crisis looks worse… 20 years ago we thought the British local surface temperature relative to the second half 19th century might go up by 0.2C per decade, but had that been true, we would be at about 1.2C now, while instead we are at 1.4C or 1.5C.” 




At the same time, low-carbon technologies have delivered far greater opportunities than were originally anticipated, only strengthening the Stern Review’s central argument, suggests Stern. 

“We did not anticipate 20 years ago that round-the-clock renewables would become cheaper than dirty energy, and we did not anticipate that the rise of electric vehicles would mean we are approaching the end of the era of the internal combustion engine,” he says. Other, harder to decarbonise sectors - including heavy industry and aviation - can follow a similar price trajectory with the same formula of helpful state regulation and investment resulting in technological improvements, he says. 


One constant across the many decades of the climate movement has been a well-funded climate-sceptic lobby, determined to dismiss the logic of the green transition and undercut its arguments. That lobby's strength has, despite ever-more alarming extreme weather, only grown in recent years - with a climate sceptic president now in the White House, and figures from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to former Labour prime minister Tony Blair (whose government commissioned the Stern Review) souring on the UK's net z

Fire has always be part of life on the grasslands, but has grown worse due to rising temperatures and severe droughts. In response, people have turned to their nomadic heritage to help tackle the blazes



By Michael O Snyder




Sodnomjamts Damchaabadgar squats in a shallow, rocky depression, working quietly with his hands. Inches above the rim of the pit, the wind whips across the grasslands. But in the marginal shelter of the dig site the air remains calm – essential for delicate operations.
Damchaabadgar, a research fellow at the Institute of Archaeology at the Mongolian Academy of Sciences, has erected a ger, a traditional nomad’s tent, nearby, which serves as his sleeping quarters and a field station.



View image in fullscreen

 
 
Two gers stand alone against the vast openness of the steppe in Eastern Mongolia. The ger – often called a yurt outside Mongolia – is a round dwelling designed to be assembled or disassembled in a matter of hours 


View image in fullscreen

 
 
Sodnomtsamts Damchaabadgar excavates a pair of skulls from a bronze age burial site in Aduun Chuluun, Töv province 
“When we examine these gravesites, we see evidence of horse domestication dating back to the middle bronze age,” he says. “We now think that the ancient peoples of Mongolia may have tamed horses far earlier than previously expected, perhaps as early as 2,000 BCE, which makes sense because horses were critical to survival on the grasslands. They gave an advantage in battle – that’s well known – but perhaps just as importantly, horses gave them the speed that they needed to escape from the grassland’s greatest natural threat: fire.”


View image in fullscreen

 
 
Fire rangers arrive on the scene of a blaze in Bayan-Ovoo, Khentii province 





View image in fullscreen


View image in fullscreen

 
 
Left: the remnants of a burned ger in Dornod province. Right: a faint scar from a recent fire crosses a rural road 


While fire has long been endemic on the steppe, the hazard has been steadily growing in the 20th and 21st centuries. The human-driven climate crisis has led to the heating and drying of the Eurasian grasslands, with a 2C rise in temperatures recorded over the last 80 years.
From 1981 to 1995, an average of 1.74 million hectares (4.3m acres) of forest and steppe was scorched each year during fire season. Then, from 1996 to 1999, more than 30m hectares was consumed by fire in four years. More recently, the fire seasons of 2022 and 2025 led to deepening public concern.

Munkhjin, from Bayan-Ovoo, shields her eyes against blowing dust

A sign in Khentii province reads: ‘You can prevent wildfires!’

articles.raw_meta: As chief US diplomat, Rubio could do great good. His pandering and neglect are a disgrace we shouldn’t ignore, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
articles.jina_text:
Viewed from the state department in Washington DC, the world is on fire – but record heatwaves are not to blame. The unresolved Iran war has badly burned Donald Trump. His military campaign conclusively failed, energy and food prices are still rising, and a Republican rout in November’s midterm elections looms. Humiliatingly, Israel this week flatly rejected his latest Gaza peace proposals, days after Trump congratulated himself on a “historic breakthrough”. In Europe, Russia’s attacks on Nato allies grow increasingly brazen, threatening a wider escalation. The Ukraine war, which Trump vowed to end, is now well into its fifth year, with civilians on both sides caught in the killing fields. And these are just the bigger firestorms. There are plenty more.
Rarely has the need for effective, professional diplomacy been more pressing. So step forward Marco Rubio, US secretary of state and chief American diplomat. These are challenges that, if successfully tackled, could propel the 55-year-old son of Cuban immigrants and the former US senator for Florida into pole position in the 2028 Republican presidential nomination race. Here is a chance for Rubio to defy critics who dismiss him as a lickspittle and Trump dogsbody, and transform himself into respected global statesman. His boss mocked him as “little Marco” and a “loser” when they were election rivals in 2016. (Rubio called him a conman.) Now is Rubio’s opportunity to go big, be brave and prove he’s a winner.



Or maybe not.
Rubio is unlike recent US secretaries of state – heavyweights such as Hillary Clinton and Antony Blinken, or John Kerry, famed for his high-energy shuttle diplomacy. Rubio has little time for “peace processes”. Instead, he projects brute US power to impose take-it-or-leave-it “solutions” that advance US interests, as defined by Trump. It’s a modern form of imperialism. Target countries have a choice: become client states, like Venezuela and, prospectively, Cuba and Greenland, or be crushed. In Iran, the policy is not regime change, let alone democratic renewal. It’s regime compliance. Rubio behaves less like a peace-broker, more like a pith-helmeted colonial viceroy demanding fealty from obsequious satraps.
Speaking in Munich in February, Rubio aired his hawkishly retro doctrine of US primacy. He lamented the decline of “the great western empires … accelerated by godless communist revolutions and anti-colonial uprisings” and warned Europe faced “civilisational erasure”. The US didn’t want milksop allies “shackled by guilt and shame” about their imperial past, he said. “We want allies who are proud of their culture and heritage … and who, together with us, are willing and able to defend it.” Here was a familiar assertion of US hegemony, but one stripped of bogus altruism and pretence. It sounded a death knell for diplomacy. Trump has attacked eight countries in the past year. Cuba, Rubio’s obsession, could be next.

Alarmed by the alarm: people react to ‘severe alert’ on phones over UK wildfires


Many complained online that piercingly loud tone was ‘overreach’ while others lamented lack of action on decarbonisation




On Friday at 7pm, Thérèse Coffey was nine miles away from a nuclear power station when her phone made a loud, piercing and very worrying sound: it was a “severe” emergency alert. “Was expecting [a] much more specific alert, not a generic message on wildfires,” the former Conservative cabinet minister said on X.
She wasn’t alone in being alarmed by the alarm sent to phones in England and Wales. In the aftermath, thousands of social media users expressed their shock at alert. Some shared funny memes and others lamented what they viewed as lack of government action on decarbonisation. Academic John Ritzema called it a “massive overreach” and said the alert system should be “be for ‘drop everything and prepare for something terrible’ situations”, something Coffey echoed, saying alerts should not become commonplace to avoid “Peter cries wolf situations”.



Even broadcasters were taken by surprise. The alert sounded live on the BBC’s The One Show, with host Ronan Kemp saying: “We’ve got some form of fire alarm going on.”
Chris Packham used the alert to plug a parliamentary petition calling for a UK-wide briefing on climate and nature risks.
The alert on Friday night came as Andy Burnham spent time in Stourbridge in the West Midlands earlier that day after homes were destroyed and residents were left injured by a series of fires. The prime minister warned that Britain “is a tinderbox right now”, with the public set for a “difficult weekend”.
It has been a record year of wildfires in England and Wales: the number so far has passed the 1,017 recorded in 2025. Fire services declared 11 major incidents in a 24-hour period starting on Thursday.
People have been urged not to light barbecues, campfires, fireworks or anything else that could spark a blaze while the wildfire risk remains high. They have also been urged to call 999 immediately if they spot a fire.

Read more
The wildfires have also prompted calls within the Labour party to accelerate action against the climate crisis. Sadiq Khan warned Burnham not to “slow down on net zero” and said the heatwave and wildfires showed the need for action on climate change. The London mayor described the planet as being in a “deeply precarious position”.

articles.jina_text:
A Shropshire vicar played a key role in a new two-part BBC documentary featuring Welsh Hollywood actor Michael Sheen's investigation into toxic waste dumps.
The Rev Paul Cawthorne, priest in charge of churches in the Hadnall area, is also a long time environmental campaigner.
He began looking into the history of the former landfill site at Stoney Hill, in Telford, where former chemical giant, Monsanto, is known to have legally dumped waste in the mid to late 1980s.
"When I found out about the Monsanto chemical dumping at Stoney Hill, I next identified Sutton Walls in Herefordshire, then Cefn Mawr in north Wales," he said.
"I then went around south Wales valleys identifying historically documented sites which needed additional testing," he added.
Cawthorne said he has been on a 20 year mission to uncover the truth.
He said that "dangerously elevated levels" of polychlorinated biphenyls - toxic man-made chemicals which don't easily break down in nature - were found in nine out of 10 sites discussed in the Buried BBC radio series.
"The results at some were literally off the scale and will have a big impact in professional circles, assuming they cannot continue to try to ignore them now," he said.
Details of Monsanto's involvement at Stoney Hill between 1985-1988, when it was managed by Shropshire County Council, was revealed in a recent Freedom of Information request.
Cawthorne has now called on the current site owners, Telford and Wrekin Council, to order a full fresh statutory investigation into the former landfill site near Coalbrookdale.
The LDRS asked Telford and Wrekin Council for a response to Cawthorne's repeated calls for an investigation.
A council spokesperson said: "Information about Stoneyhill landfill site's active management plan is available on the council's website."
The council took over the management of the former landfill site in 1998 and states on its website there is "no evidence in the records received from Shropshire County Council that toxic materials or waste were tipped in Stoneyhill landfill."
It also carries out regular testing and it states these have not identified any cause for concern.
The council's website adds that a detailed assessment and review was carried out by the Environment Agency in 2008 and "as a result the site is not considered a harm to the local environment."
For the documentary, he put his focus on the former activities of Monsanto, which produced a range of chemicals at factories in Newport, south Wales, and Ruabon, near Chirk, before the disposal legislation began to tighten in 1974.
Buried with Michael Sheen, comes to BBC Two, BBC One Wales and BBC iPlayer from Monday 17 August.
This news was gathered by the Local Democracy Reporting Service which covers councils and other public service organisations.

articles.jina_text:
GB News hosts Dawn Neesom and Sam Francis have reacted to the "terrifying" exposure by GB News Reporter Alice Tomlinson on the takeover of London's iconic red buses by Chinese manufacturer BYD.
Detailing her report on GB News Breakfast, Alice told Dawn and Sam: "I did this investigation through an FOI request to TfL, so in 2020, there were 261 BYD buses in Londons electric vehicle bus fleet, and that has surged by 359 per cent in the last five years. 


"So now as of March 2025, that stands at almost 1,200 buses. BYD, which stands for 'Build Your Dreams' is a Chinese manufacturer. And interestingly, they have been designated by the US as a "Chinese military company". 
"BYD rejects that designation, but what it infers is that this is a company that is now essentially kind of has fingers in lots of pies in terms of London's transport system."
Reacting to the report, Dawn said: "Absolutely terrifying, it's frightening. One of the most popular e-vehicles on the road now is manufactured in China, by the Chinese, and we obviously have the mega embassy opening in London as well."
Sam then added: "It'll be interesting to find out whether it's just the capital or whether there's more widespread across the country as well, because e-vehicles are rolling out more and more and more.
"I mean, you just look around this studio, I wonder how much is probably Chinese controlled?"
Dawn concluded: "Phones, laptops, cameras, who knows?"
GB News put these exclusive findings to TfL, asking specifically whether it or its subcontracted bus operators manage these software updates and whether BYD notifies them before updates are applied.
A spokesman said: "All buses entering service in London must meet our robust technical requirements and we are committed to rigorous testing."

Rail passengers face slower train journeys and a reduced timetable if summer heatwaves become more frequent with climate change.



The train derailment near Lewes in East Sussex on Thursday – the hottest day of the year – has sparked fears about the potential impact of higher temperatures on the rail network.



A second derailment happened less than 24 hours later in Essex on Friday, leading to further concern that parts of the rail infrastructure may be struggling to cope with intense weather.



The Labour Government may have to spend more upgrading infrastructure to help the network adapt to the changing climate, experts told The i Paper.

articles.jina_text:
Rail passengers face slower train journeys and a reduced timetable if summer heatwaves become more frequent with climate change. 
The train derailment near Lewes in East Sussex on Thursday – the hottest day of the year – has sparked fears about the potential impact of higher temperatures on the rail network. 
A second derailment happened less than 24 hours later in Essex on Friday, leading to further concern that parts of the rail infrastructure may be struggling to cope with intense weather.

 
The Labour Government may have to spend more upgrading infrastructure to help the network adapt to the changing climate, experts told The i Paper. 
The cause of Thursday’s overturned Southern Rail commuter carriages – which left 20 people injured, including two serious injuries – is not yet known. 
The cause of the partial derailment of a Greater Anglia train near Wickford in Essex is also unknown. The rear carriages were derailed in an upright position shortly after 2pm on Friday, but no injuries were initially reported. 
But heat expansion causing rail lines to buckle is one possibility that will be looked at by investigators, said industry experts.



 
Footage from Lewes revealed a section of track that the overturned train had passed over was badly warped. However, the derailing itself could have caused the movement, said experts. 
Painting rails white and ‘re-stressing’ track 
Network Rail has explained that rails are “stressed” – carefully adjusting their length to reduce tension – to help them resist the effects of high temperatures. 
“In Britain, our rails have a target stress-free temperature of 27 degrees,” Network Rail said in a post on X last month. 
Re-stressing the network for the far-higher temperatures seen this summer has not been deemed necessary because the lines also have to deal with cold temperatures in the British winter. 
However, Network Rail said it was taking steps to adjust to more severe summers: including painting rails white to reflect sunlight, fitting additional anchors to sleepers and re-stressing sections of rail lines. 

Officials investigate overturned carriages after derailment near Lewes.(Photo: James Manning/PA Wire) 
The nation’s network operator also pointed out that train speed restrictions are needed in hot weather to reduce the impact on the lines. It can mean fewer trains to avoid lines become overcrowded. 
Phil Blythe CBE, professor of intelligent transport systems at Newcastle University, said it could take “a decade or more” to adapt the UK’s rail infrastructure to extreme heat, he said.



 
Tough decisions will have to be made on priorities because “there isn’t much money around”, warned Prof Blyth – who leads the DARe hub of academics and transport industry leaders looking at climate resilience. 
Slower trains and reduced services in summer 
Passengers could face both “slower trains and reduced service” in the summers ahead “until a lot of these improvements can be made”, said Prof Blythe.

articles.raw_content:
Like all Prime Ministers, Andy Burnham is finding that events can upset even the best laid plans.



On Friday the PM was diverted from his cost of living tour around the UK, to view the devastation in Stourbridge, where 19 homes were completely destroyed after wild grassland fires caught up with suburbia.



The scenes of flames completely gutting detached and semi-detached UK homes were apocalyptic, and the PM responded by temporarily banning disposable barbecues, announcing extra resources for firefighters and sending an emergency phone alert warning against “any activity that could start a fire”.

‘In the heatwaves, it’s crucial’: the fight to save France’s rural swimming pools


Ageing facilities offering daily refuge face funding threat as record temperatures parch the countryside




Suzy Bernard took a breath and jumped into the deep end of her village swimming pool with a splash.
“There’s a wonderful feeling of wellbeing in the water,” said the former hospital healthcare assistant, who recently learned to swim aged 75 and was now gliding along with her daughter and grandson.



View image in fullscreen
Suzy Bernard: ‘We’ll fight to make sure this pool survives’
The municipal swimming pool, bordered by shady oak trees in the village of Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, in western France, has been the Bernard family’s daily refuge from the sweltering heatwaves this summer. Bernard is a member of the village collective, Touche Pas à Ma Piscine (Hands Off My Pool), campaigning to defend the Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe facility and calling for more government support for rural swimming pools. “We’ll fight to make sure this pool survives and stays open,” she said.


As a summer of record temperatures parched much of the French countryside, local village swimming pools, with cheap entry tickets, have often been the only shelter from the heatwaves for rural families on low incomes who cannot afford to go on holiday or who live in heat-trap homes. The pools are also crucial for teaching rural communities to swim. A total of 274 people died from drowning in France between 1 May and 15 July this year, with most deaths occurring when people jumped into rivers and waterways to cool down.





Families enjoy local swimming pools in western France


But France’s ageing rural swimming pools, many of which were built in 1970s, are in crisis as village mayors with shrinking budgets struggle to pay the high running costs and some pools are forced to close owing to lack of funds.
In Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, a village of 3,200 people in Les Hauts-d’Anjou, a farming area of the Pays de la Loire, the new mayor, Véronique Langlais, said she was determined to keep running the village pool that opened in 1973, despite an annual cost of at least €100,000 (£85,000) to the town hall’s modest budget. Three other rural pools had closed in the surrounding countryside, making this the only pool in a radius of about 20 miles.


View image in fullscreen
Véronique Langlais, mayor of Hauts-d’Anjou, in the changing rooms of the Hauts-d’Anjou swimming pool

articles.jina_text:
Disposable barbecues have been temporarily banned from sale over fears they pose a "significant risk to the public" as drought and heatwave conditions continue to grip the UK.
They have been the cause of "a number of serious wildfires across the country over the summer months", the government said. 
A potential ban was first discussed at an emergency Cobra meeting in response to record temperatures earlier this week. The public have been urged not to light an open fires and to dispose of cigarettes carefully.
Meanwhile Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the country is like "a tinderbox", as 200 personnel have now been deployed to help emergency teams tackling wildfires around the country. 






Burnham says UK is like a 'tinderbox' as West Midlands crews tackle multiple fires for second day



Watch: 'Carnage' in Stourbridge as houses destroyed by fire





20 hours ago


What is causing the summer wildfires?





25 July




As part of the military deployment, Gurkha logistics teams equipped with water tankers and military engineers are now assisting fire services in South Wales. 
Andy Burnham has promised more military personnel will be deployed elsewhere if needed.
Crews in England and Wales tackled multiple blazes on Friday and an emergency alert was sent to millions of phones.
A total of 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), which matches last year's record.
As well as devastating blazes in the West Midlands which saw dozens of homes destroyed, fire crews have been in action across the two countries.
In Wales, a major incident was declared near Llandovery, Carmarthenshire, after dozens of homes were evacuated and roads closed.
In Hampshire, firefighters have spent a sixth day tackling a wildfire in the New Forest, which broke out on Sunday.
Sixteen emergencies were tackled by Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service on Thursday afternoon, including a fire at Mousehold Heath in the city.
On Friday evening, an emergency alert was sent to mobile phones warning of a "very high risk of wildfires nationally" across England and Wales.
The message asked residents, landowners and visitors to not undertake any activity that could cause a fire "including disposable barbecues, firepits, garden incinerators of fireworks".
It was the most extensive use of the system to date, according to the government.









Disposable barbecues "cannot be considered a safe product" in the current conditions and they "must not be made available for sale either in store or online at the current time" in Great Britain, according to the advice published by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST)., external
The ban applies to England, Scotland and Wales, but not Northern Ireland.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the measures were "common-sense steps to protect lives and the environment."

Burnham announces £65m for drought-hit farmers after Labour pressure


PM steps up climate response with measures including better water access and support for building farm reservoirs




Farmers must not carry the risks of the climate crisis alone, Andy Burnham has said, as he announced £65m of funding to help them manage the devastating drought.
The prime minister is stepping up his response to the immediate climate crisis after facing a backlash from his own MPs and Labour’s grassroots for not addressing the climate crisis despite wildfires tearing through Britain and a drought affecting food producers. Labour MPs argued Burnham had taken too long to talk about the climate crisis and had not made it a priority.

Some farmers have had to harvest their crops early, while others are seeing low-quality produce and low yields. Most of the £65m will go to the sustainable farming incentive (SFI), which pays farmers in England to support nature. Officials have said this extra £50m will bring the total SFI budget to £290m, with extra money prioritised for areas of greatest need during the drought.
Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting on extreme heat, wildfires and drought this week. Downing Street is seeking to establish a cross-government response to the drought, bringing together action on farming, water and infrastructure, including more flexibility for food producers. Farmers who are paid to look after nature on parts of their land and are usually barred from cutting or grazing it until later in the year are now able to do so where grass is scarce, without losing payments.


View image in fullscreen
Andy Burnham and the West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker (third from right), met fire service staff in Stourbridge on Friday Photograph: Peter Byrne/AFP/Getty Images
Farmers will also get £15m in support for building on-farm reservoirs to provide supplies during future dry summers.  However, campaigners have warned this £15m is reallocated money from existing funds and will only fund a “fraction” of reservoirs needed. They will get improved access to water through simpler arrangements around how much they can take from the environment and changes to the speed at which licences are given, making it easier for farmers to use water where it is most needed.


Burnham is to visit a farm in the south-west of England on Saturday and is expected to say: “I am meeting with farmers here in the south-west who brought in the earliest harvest of their working lives and watched the yield come in well down on what it should be.
