articles.title: Andy Burnham sends heatwave wildfire mobile phone alerts to millions of Londoners as city frazzles in 34C
articles.raw_rss: The capital sizzled with highs of 34.3 on Friday, the day after the mercury hit 38.1C in Kew Gardens
articles.raw_meta: The capital sizzled with highs of 34.3 on Friday, the day after the mercury hit 38.1C in Kew Gardens
articles.jina_text:
An emergency alert from the Government was sent to millions across the UK on Friday evening, as London continued to experience baking heatwave conditions.




The alert, which began appearing on mobile devices from 7pm, warned people not to light anything that could spark a wildfire, including barbecues, campfires, and fireworks.








It comes as Friday became a record-breaking 10th day in 2026 where temperatures have exceeded 35C or more in the UK, according to the Met Office.


A screenshot of the emergency alert
PA




The capital sizzled with highs of 34.3 on Friday, the day after the hottest temperature of the year in the UK was recorded, with the mercury hitting 38.1C in Kew Gardens on Thursday.




The alert read: “There is a very high risk of wildfires nationally. Residents, landowners and visitors should not undertake any activity that could start a fire, including disposable barbecues, firepits, garden incinerators or fireworks.




“Even a small flame can rapidly develop into a major wildfire placing lives, homes, businesses and emergency responders at risk. Follow official updates and report signs of fire immediately by calling 999.”




London’s parks have been turned into “tinderbox” parched lands where fires can easily spread, including a wildfire which tore through Hornchurch Country Park on Friday evening.


An aerial view of a parched golf course in in Mitcham, London
Getty




The London Fire Brigade (LFB) confirmed that 14 fire engines and around 90 firefighters responded to the blaze, which produced a significant amount of smoke.












Sir Sadiq Khan has urged Londoners to create fire breaks in their gardens to protect their homes, while the London Fire Brigade (LFB) has also warned of the dangers that major blazes could start in people’s gardens.




More than 1,000 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), the same as last year’s record-breaking total. 








Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh, the First Secretary of State, said that the alert was “the most extensive use of the UK’s emergency alert system in response to an active incident”.









The alert played havoc with TV and radio broadcasts, with the One Show’s 20th anniversary special episode disrupted just minutes after starting.

Many in Wales were confused by the alerts - where they were sent in Welsh.

The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, speaks to staff during a visit to the Met Office weather and climate service in Exeter on Friday. Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/AFP/Getty Images


Burnham criticised for EV and North Sea approach amid climate crisis


Cut in electric vehicle sales targets could add millions of tonnes of CO2 to emissions in UK, say green campaigners




Andy Burnham has been criticised for moving to cut electric vehicle (EV) sales targets and accept North Sea drilling at a time of devastating wildfires caused by the climate emergency.
The prime minister for the first time acknowledged on Friday that the climate crisis was behind hundreds of wildfires that have ripped across the parts of the UK.

The scale of the disaster has prompted the government to bring in the military, ban the sale of disposable barbecues and activate the national alert system to issue safety advice to people across England and Wales in areas at risk on Friday night.
However, Burnham was also accused of failing to take the push for net zero seriously enough, as the government took steps towards watering down EV targets on the same day.


View image in fullscreen
Several homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands were destroyed as a result of wildfires this week. Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images
The government on Friday launched a consultation on cutting the target for new EVs to as little as 50% of all new cars in 2030, down from 80% under existing rules, in proposals that could add millions of tonnes a year to the UK’s carbon dioxide emissions.


The consultation will include several options, including leaving the headline target unchanged, or cutting it to 70%, 60% or 50%.
In a video from the West Midlands, where homes have been destroyed and dozens of people injured, Burnham appeared to acknowledge the seriousness of the climate crisis. “We cannot accept this as the new normal,” he said. “This isn’t happening in isolation.
“Much of England and Wales is in drought and we are in another period of extreme heat. Farmers are watching crops fail and firefighters have faced hundreds of wildfires in a matter of weeks. This is what climate change looks like, here and now.”


View image in fullscreen
Andy Burnham and the West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, right, with the West Midlands chief fire officer, Simon Tuhill, during a visit to Stourbridge on Friday. Photograph: Peter Byrne/Reuters


But in a broadcast interview, he also defended his “pragmatic” approach on extracting oil and gas from the North Sea. His government will shortly have to decide whether to allow new drilling at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields, with a consultation on the former closing on Monday.

‘It’s due to climate’: the people of Stourbridge on the town’s wildfires


Thursday has been described by residents as ‘horrendous’, ‘distressing’ and ‘one of the scariest days of my life’




People in Stourbridge have described the fires that devastated more than a dozen homes as “horrendous” and “distressing”, with one describing blazes that surpassed the height of residential houses.
Multiple fires spread across the West Midlands on Thursday as temperatures reached record highs of 38.1C in the UK, during the country’s fifth consecutive heatwave.

Fifty-four people, including 19 who were taken to hospital, were treated at eight different fires on Thursday, West Midlands ambulance service said, with the fire service confirming 19 homes in Stourbridge, a market town in Dudley, had been fully destroyed and an additional 18 damaged.
During a visit to Stourbridge on Friday, Andy Burnham said the UK was like a “tinderbox” and announced the commission of firefighting planes to tackle future wildfires. “I’ve never seen scenes like this anywhere in Britain,” he told the BBC.
The Guardian spoke to people who were forced to hurriedly evacuate from their homes in Stourbridge on Thursday, as a wildfire spread near the town’s golf course.


View image in fullscreen
From left: Andy Hobbs, Gemma Hobbs and neighbour John Bairner, were evacuated from their homes on Osmaston Road. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian
They repeatedly praised the support and efforts of local authorities and neighbours, but are yet to return home, with some staying at a nearby hotel or a makeshift evacuation centre that had been set up at a local boarding school.


Gemma Hobbs, 46, and her partner, Andy, 61, were evacuated from their home on Osmaston Road on Thursday, as the wildfires raged over a mile away. Andy described seeing a house in flames.
Gemma said: “I looked out the windows and all I could see was thick black smoke. My husband came home in a bit of a flap and said: ‘We’ve got to get out. We’ve got to get out immediately.’”
Andy added: “It’s just the fact you don’t expect something to be as exponential as this so quickly. From the span of the area, it’s over 40 acres, that’s what we’ve been told.”
Gareth Jones, 59, was providing shelter to his neighbour John Bairner, who had to be evacuated overnight and said it was a “scene of devastation”, calling the wildfire “terrifying”.
“It was probably one of the scariest days of my life yesterday,” he said. “It was just the speed at which it spread, it was devastating. Absolutely frightening how quickly it spread. Within an hour. It’s a major event.”

articles.title: Electric vehicle sales targets could be cut after pressure from car makers
articles.raw_rss: The government says it is considering cutting the new electric car sales target from 80% to 50% by 2030.
articles.raw_meta: The government says it is considering cutting the new electric car sales target from 80% to 50% by 2030.
articles.jina_text:
The UK's electric vehicle (EV) sales target could be cut after the government launched a review following pressure from car makers.
Currently, manufacturers must ensure a percentage of the cars they sell each year are zero emissions, with the target rising each year to reach 80% by 2030.
The government has now said it is considering cutting that figure to as far as 50% of all sales by the end of the decade, which it will consult on until late October.
Environmental groups have argued that watering down the target undermines the UK's long-term climate goals.
Under the current policy, known as the ZEV mandate, the percentage of new car sales that need to be EVs increases each year, from 33% for 2026 until it reaches 80% by 2030. It started at 22% in 2024.
An outright ban on selling purely petrol or diesel cars past 2030 will stay in place, something that Labour promised in its election manifesto.
However the changes now being consulted on could allow car makers to sell more hybrid vehicles as a proportion of the UK's overall sales.
That means if the government drops pure electric sales targets to 50%, the other 50% would need to be hybrid.
Another option would be keeping the target at 80% but with flexibility for car makers extending as far as 2034.
A longer term deadline for phasing out new hybrid sales would also remain in place for 2035.
The policy on EV sales has already changed a lot over the years.
A ban on selling new petrol and diesel vehicles by 2030 was first announced by Boris Johnson when he was prime minister, then pushed back to 2035 by his successor Rishi Sunak.
Sunak also introduced more gradual targets for EV sales under the ZEV mandate.
Labour has previously accused previous Conservative governments of "moving goalposts on phase out dates".
It comes after motor industry figures urged ministers to ease the targets, arguing that demand for electric vehicles isn't yet high enough, and meeting them is costing manufacturers too much money.
That is despite electric cars making up a quarter of total sales in the UK over the first seven months of the year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT).
The Climate Change Committee, which advises the government, has said switching from diesel and petrol engines to EVs will be the most effective way of cutting carbon emissions over the next decade.
Transport Secretary, Heidi Alexander said on Friday: "It's right we keep targets under review to ensure they're practical and back British industry. 
"The end goal hasn't changed – but we need to take business with us on the journey, and that's exactly what we're doing today, by making sure industry has the chance to shape how we get there."
Lisa Brankin, managing director of Ford of Britain, welcomed the government's "willingness to listen" to car makers, adding: "It is vital to give the industry and customers the certainty that we need."

The Great Barrier Reef isn’t dead yet. According to News Corp that makes climate science a ‘pseudo-religion’

Graham Readfearn






‘High coral cover is evidence of recovery and resilience, not evidence that the disturbances causing mortality didn’t happen,’ scientist says 
 
 





The Australian newspaper appeared to think it had a slam-dunk this week with a front page story pointing to official government data which showed “the Great Barrier Reef is refusing to die” despite decades of warnings that global heating would cause its demise.
In an editorial to back its reporting, the newspaper claimed the “continued good health” of the reef was a “welcome reminder that physics rather than the pseudo-religion of climate change doom still holds sway over the natural order.”

Scientific-based assessments of risks facing the reef from global heating were wrong, it seemed, and the data and the physics showed it.
But the Australian Institute of Marine Science – the agency upon which the outlet pinned its claims – has told this column the newspaper was guilty of “oversimplified framing” and that its recent surveys did not contradict warnings about the risks to the reef from the climate crisis.


“The scientific concern is not that the GBR should already have disappeared, it’s whether reefs will have sufficiently long periods between disturbances for full ecosystem recovery,” the institute said.
The Guardian sent questions to The Australian but received no response.
‘Volatility is evidence of ecosystem instability’
The Australian’s report leaned heavily on the latest annual results of the institute’s long-term monitoring program – a 40-year effort which, between August 2025 and June 2026, took detailed records from surveys of 121 reefs.
The program reports annually on levels of coral cover – that is, how much live hard coral is growing on reef areas – which was at “near record levels” across the reef, The Australian reported.

The Prime Minister was speaking as he visited the scene of a fire in Stourbridge in the West Midlands, where residents were forced to evacuate.

        







The Prime Minister said the drought could be followed by flooding as heavy rain falls of dry ground (Jacob King/PA)




David Lynch
2 minutes ago







Flooding could follow the wildfires sweeping the country, Andy Burnham has said.




The Prime Minister made the warning as he visited the scene of a fire in Stourbridge in the West Midlands, where residents were forced to evacuate.




A total of 54 people have been treated by paramedics, including 19 who were admitted to hospital, after wildfires broke out across the region.








Speaking to broadcasters on Friday afternoon, the Prime Minister paid tribute to the work of firefighters, and added: “We might be in for a wet autumn and winter straight after this, because of El Nino and some of the issues there, which was reported to Cobra. So, after fire could come floods.




“We have to face up to the changing climate. I think we need a different debate about that. There’s no point denying where we are. We need to face up to it. We need more clean energy. We need to see that transition accelerate. Those are all of the issues that, you know, are right now in discussion.




“But the Cobra meeting earlier this week, I think has enabled us to mobilise resource today to individuals, to communities, and to our fire and rescue services, and we’re very, very grateful to them.”




Mr Burnham later told the BBC that the Met Office believes the dry spell will last until the end of September, when some rain is expected.




He also told the broadcaster: “Maybe some rainfall, but not as much as we need, and then we are heading straight into a very, very wet latter part of the year, where the risk of flooding will be maybe greater because of the dry ground conditions.


Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited the scene of a fire in Stourbridge in the West Midlands on Friday (Peter Byrne/PA)
PA Wire




“At the moment, fire and rescue services are not set up for flooding properly, and again, these are questions that I have to take away, and you know I won’t shy away from them.”













Met Office climate spokesman Grahame Madge said it was a “tremendously tricky job” to work out which climate drivers will be the most dominant ahead of autumn and winter.




Mr Madge told the Press Association: “But the Prime Minister is perfectly right in what he said, in terms of there is a known association between strong El Nino events and a wet autumn.









“It’s important to highlight that El Nino is a pattern of natural climate variability – it’s not linked to climate change per se.




“It can accentuate other climate signals, such as a warmer atmosphere, it can hold more moisture, all of that, but it’s not an artefact of climate change itself.”

articles.jina_text:
Five key reservoirs across England and Wales are “exceptionally low” as drought and extreme heat piles pressure on public water supply that is likely to continue into the autumn.
Most of Europe has endured back-to-back climate crisis-driven heatwaves this summer. The extreme heat, coupled with strikingly little rainfall, means almost three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales is now in drought.

Environment Agency data from 11 August shows five key reservoirs are now “exceptionally low”.
Wimbleball reservoir, operated by South West Water, is less than half full, at 46%. The other four that are “exceptionally low” are Clatworthy in Somerset (48%), Hanningfield in Essex (56%), Clywedog in Powys (56%), and the Dove group in Derbyshire (69%).

Across England, total reservoir levels have fallen to 66%, down from 69% last week and nearly 14 percentage points lower than expected for this time of year. Of the 32 reservoirs the Environment Agency classifies as strategically important or geographically representative, just four are classed as at normal levels.


These are Draycote Water in Warwickshire, Bewl in Kent, Roadford in Devon and Vyrnwy in Powys.
Reservoirs are essential for the security of water supply, providing drinking water to millions of people.
In its latest summary published on Thursday, the National Hydrological Monitoring Programme said aridity in July had been “unprecedented” and that “widespread below-normal to exceptionally low” water flows were likely to persist well into the autumn, with “further deterioration” likely.


View image in fullscreen
Woodhead reservoir near Manchester. Photograph: Jon Super/AP


Alastair Chisholm, the lead for water policy, regulation and governance at the consultancy firm Arup, said with three droughts recorded in the past five years, the country was in “new territory”.
During last year’s drought, reservoir levels also fell to extremely low levels. By this time last year, the Pennines group and Yorkshire group reservoirs were less than 39% full, and experts say this cumulative impact is of particular concern.
England and Wales rely on on reservoirs filling up over the winter – and this year’s particularly wet winter has meant the situation this summer is not as bad as it could have been. “If we do get a dry winter this time round, then that will be very concerning for the government,” Chisholm said.

Prof Liz Bentley, the chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, said the key concern now was how long the dry weather would continue.
“There is very little rain forecast over the next couple of weeks and that is more the concern. If we go through autumn and winter and have low rainfall, we could have real trouble,” she said.
Mark Smith, the chair of the Chartered Institution of Water and Environmental Management’s water resources specialist panel, said that while winter rain helped, “ultimately you can only store so much”.

articles.jina_text:
Firefighters across France and in central England struggled against multiple fires Friday as a new wave of record-breaking heat baked a swath of Europe, their task further complicated by exceptionally parched landscapes.
With France experiencing its driest year ever, a new fire raced through woodlands overnight in the Landes region on the southwest coast. The blaze forced more than 500 people to evacuate their homes in the town of Luglon as hundreds of firefighters deployed to the area, the regional administration said Friday.
It’s one of several fires scorching forests around France this week, including in normally cooler and wetter regions in the north and Brittany. A historic fire devoured forests near Bordeaux last month and pushed a quarter of a million people from their homes.





After the U.K. recorded its hottest day of the year, wildfires raced across the West Midlands and saw several houses burned to the ground. They have been “one of the most significant” incidents the region’s fire service has ever dealt with, chief fire officer Simon Tuhill said. 
Some 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data from the National Fire Chiefs Council.

The fires came on the hottest day of the year, when temperatures reached 38.1 degrees Celsius (100.6 degrees Fahrenheit) in west London.


In France, temperatures Thursday approached 41 C (106 F) in several areas, from Aquitaine in the southwest to the Rhone River valley in the east, according to the national weather service. They were forecast to reach similar levels Friday before dropping over the weekend. 
The historic temperatures are linked to human-caused climate change, and are hitting countries more designed for long cold seasons and ill-equipped for this sort of heat, with limited air conditioning.



In northern Greece, more than 300 vacationers and residents were evacuated by sea Thursday after a wildfire swept through a pine forest and threatened seaside homes, authorities said.

articles.title: What the price of a cucumber tells you about the future of your food shop
articles.raw_rss: There are a handful of swaps to make if you want to keep a lid on your shopping bill
articles.raw_content:
Of all the measures you might take to see how this summer’s climate change-powered heatwaves are wrecking the UK, the price of a cucumber is one of the less obvious. But it is one of the most revealing.



The wholesale price of cucumbers has more than doubled since the first UK heatwave struck in May, according to new government figures. And savoy cabbages have jumped by 14 per cent, in what farmers are calling a “disastrous summer for British brassicas”.



“Fields of broccoli, cauliflower and cabbage have now stopped growing and have become dormant,” the Brassica Growers Association has reported – one of many dire warnings of late from UK farmers working across fruit, vegetables, cereals and livestock, as The i Paper has reported.



After the driest July on record in England and Wales – and with 45 million people now living in drought conditions in the UK – they are expected to see their worst harvest on record this summer.

People in Jorhat, Assam, wade through floodwaters with animals and belongings salvaged after flooding in late July.  Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
People in Jorhat, Assam, wade through floodwaters with animals and belongings salvaged after flooding in late July.  Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images


‘We feared we’d all be drowned’: the Indian floods that killed more than 100 and left thousands homeless


More than 2,600 villages have been flooded in Assam this year, in a climate disaster made worse by uncontrolled deforestation and mining in the region




It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.

“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.


View image in fullscreen
Gitali Phukon in flood water outside her house on 28 July, a week after the village was flooded.  Photograph: Gitali Phukon/The Migration Story
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.

articles.title: My one-year postgrad degree will cost me £30,000 and leave me struggling to buy a home
articles.raw_rss: James Fenneberg, 45, says the money he is putting into his education could otherwise have gone towards building greater financial security
articles.raw_content:
At 45, James Fenneberg is going back to university for a postgraduate degree, and anticipates it will cost him around £30,000 in fees, renting, travel and materials costs.



James is studying a postgraduate degree in environmental architecture at the Royal College of Art (RCA) in London, starting in September, but worries the cost of the degree will lead to him struggling to buy a property in the south of England, where he wants to live.



Though he will get a student loan, it will only cover around £13,000 of his fees – and he’ll be left repaying the cost for up to 30 years, at a rate of 6 per cent on all his earnings over £21,000.





It also won’t cover his living costs and so bar a £5,000 bursary, he will be left dipping into inheritance he received from a family member – which he’d previously earmarked for a house purchase of his own.



He plans to work during his degree if he can, and hopes the qualification will allow him to find employment as a designer focused on climate change. He says the course is “unique”, which is why he is not considering studying in a cheaper city.



But he is still concerned about how the burden of the debt and upfront costs will affect him in the future, highlighting the dilemmas many who take on higher education debt face.



James currently lives in Thurrock, Kent, but will have to move to London for his qualification, which will cost him around £1,000 a month in rent and bills.

articles.jina_text:
Orangutans rescued from wildlife traffickers face a new threat from the record number of fires that have broken out in Indonesia in recent weeks.
Flames have come within metres of an animal rehabilitation centre in West Kalimantan as hot, dry and windy conditions have been amplified by a powerful El Niño and the human-driven climate crisis.

In the first 13 days of August, Indonesia registered more than three times more forest fire hotspots than in the whole of the same month last year. This followed a record number of blazes between January and July.
West Kalimantan has been at the epicentre. After 40 days without rain, there have been dozens of severe outbreaks of fire in the region.


View image in fullscreen
Orangutans at the Yiari rehabilitation centre. Photograph: Yiari
Flames threatened the Yiari orangutan rehabilitation centre this week. The fire moved rapidly from 1km away to within 100 metres of the perimeter within days, prompting staff to relocate the 60 resident orangutans to enclosures in the middle of the centre.







‘Should we leave them to die?’ The battle over how to save orangutans from the curse of palm oil

Read more
Indonesia authorities have water-bombed the forest to try to control the blaze, and teams from the centre joined the firefighting efforts as the air quality worsened, posing a threat to animals and the wider ecosystem.


The centre’s director, Dr Karmele Llano Sánchez, said in her latest update that battling the fire had been relentless. “We were fighting it until 3am, but this morning it has reignited. The teams are working round the clock but they are exhausted.”
The situation had reportedly stabilised as of Thursday evening, with all the animals safe, but the meteorological agency has said the hot, dry conditions are likely to continue and could lead to more outbreaks.
Indonesian authorities have urged people to avoid setting fires and to remain vigilant because the peak of the fire season is usually in September and October.
Yiari is seeking funds for more firefighting equipment. It warned of the growing threat earlier this year after a fire started for land clearing spread into one of its ecosystem restoration sites.

Romania shuts its last nuclear reactor as drought-hit Danube river drops to record low


Cernavoda shutdown poses immediate problems for Moldova, which relies on Romanian power ​to cover its own electricity shortages




Romania has been forced to shut down the last working ⁠reactor at its only nuclear plant after drought caused the Danube river to fall to record lows – a rare move that will immediately affect power supplies in neighbouring Moldova.
Drought and record-low water levels have deepened fears of an energy crisis across Europe, which is facing a new summer heatwave.

The drought-hit Danube, whose waters cool the Romanian plant in Cernavoda, already forced Nucelarelectrica to shut down ⁠one reactor ​in late July.






Europe’s rivers are running dry, and the knock-on effects are disastrous
Yiannis Baboulias


Read more
On Thursday the company said it needed to shut the second reactor “due to the significant and ongoing drop” in the river’s water level, and it did not foresee a restart in within the next 10 days. Nuclearelectrica’s two 706-megawatt reactors account for 20% of the country’s power ⁠output.
Romania has declared a state of energy emergency throughout August and asked companies and households to reduce consumption during peak hours.
Shutting down the reactor posed immediate problems for Moldova, Romania’s eastern neighbour, ⁠which has also endured low river levels and relies on Romanian power ​to cover up to 60% ​of its own electricity shortages.
With Romanian ​imports now unavailable, Moldova faces the prospect of increased purchases from Ukraine, ​if Kyiv can supply the ‌power, buying more ​expensive power from ​western countries or imposing rolling power cuts.


“I think we should be ready for a worsening situation, including power outages, although it’s hard to say for sure right now,” Moldovan energy expert Sergiu Tofilat told Radio Chisinau.
Romania’s energy ministry said it had ⁠turned on a 330-megawatt lignite-fired power plant, adding it was also relying on increased ​wind generation and hydro power – based ‌on available water in reservoirs – to ‌make up for shortages.
It has warned that as a last resort, large industrial users would have to face restrictions in the evening hours to save electricity. In early August, the government said carmakers Dacia and Ford would pause production in the country until 19 August to help with the power deficit.

articles.title: Human errors more to blame than climate crisis for devastating Assam floods
articles.raw_rss: Scientists seek to explain how routine monsoon rains turned into a disaster that has killed 103 people and displaced hundreds of thousands
articles.raw_meta: Scientists seek to explain how routine monsoon rains turned into a disaster that has killed 103 people and displaced hundreds of thousands
articles.jina_text:
The floods that have killed 103 people in the north-eastern Indian state of Assam this summer were not made worse by the climate crisis, but rather more immediate human errors such as unchecked deforestation and poor flood defences, a new analysis has found. 
The death toll continued to rise in Assam in Thursday’s update on the flooding, which began in late June across the northern part of the state, with multiple rivers remaining above danger levels. The floods have displaced more than 700,000 people and submerged vast stretches of farmland. Although many residents have begun returning to their homes as floodwaters recede, at least 49,000 remain housed in 125 relief camps and distribution centres, officials said earlier this week.
The loss of animal life has also been stark, with tens of thousands of farm animals and pets washed away, according to the Assam State Disaster Management Authority. With cattle sheds and grazing land badly inundated, the floods will have a long-lasting impact on livelihoods in a region heavily dependent on livestock for incomes, said Sneha Ganguly of the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, a co-author of the new study.





The floods also exposed weaknesses in Assam’s healthcare system, cutting off primary care clinics behind submerged roads, interrupting medicine supplies to people with long-term conditions and raising the risk of disease outbreaks in crowded relief camps.
The rainfall that set off the flooding was ordinary by the standards of the region, according to World Weather Attribution, an international team that assesses the role of global warming in extreme weather. 

Downpours of that size are expected roughly every one to two years, they found. However, what turned routine monsoon rain into a disaster that displaced hundreds of thousands and submerged 45,000 hectares of cropland was the state of the land it fell on. 


"Unplanned urbanisation, deforestation, poor drainage, inadequate structural flood management measures, and other anthropogenic changes now outweigh natural rainfall variability in explaining flood frequency," said Ms Ganguly.
"While climate change is making life harder for most Indians, not every disaster is a climate change disaster," said Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at the Centre for Environmental Policy at Imperial College London and another co-author. 



"The devastating flooding in Assam was instead driven by extreme human exposure, environmental degradation, and infrastructure limitations."
Assam lies in the floodplain of the Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers in Asia, which rises on the Tibetan plateau and descends through the eastern Himalayas carrying enormous quantities of sediment.

articles.jina_text:
Adding huge quantities of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere is set to cause the Earth’s forests to wither and die rather than flourish, according to a new study that counters erroneous claims that fossil fuel pollution will green the planet.
An analysis of fossilized leaf cells from a period known as the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (or PETM), which occurred about 56m years ago, has helped reconstruct how the world’s forests responded when planet-heating gases were previously being released at a rapid rate.

The current galloping pace of carbon emissions from the burning of fossil fuels is unmatched in historic and prehistoric records but the PETM, when huge amounts of carbon were released over a 130,000-year period and the world heated up by as much as 8C (14F), is the closest comparison.
The authors of the new paper found this prehistoric change caused a retreat in the forests that blanketed the Paleocene-Eocene world, causing them to die off as the Earth browned rather than greened, a finding they state has “chilling implications” for today’s world.


View image in fullscreen
Fragments of fossilized leaves like these helped the authors re-create the forest canopies of 56m years ago. Photograph: Dr Regan Dunn
“What we see is that as the carbon dioxide ramped up, the forests became very dense but then subsequently collapsed, opening up dramatically,” said Regan Dunn, a researcher at La Brea Tar Pits and the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, who led the study.


“Around 60% of the biomass of the standing vegetation was gone; it was a huge loss. This should be a concern because the rate of carbon release has never been higher than now.”
Dun added: “Forests are some of our best friends and allies but we are already seeing them die back, be cut down and consumed by wildfires. It’s happening quickly; every summer the change seems faster and faster.”







Trees may store less planet-heating carbon than hoped, study suggests

Read more
Plants like trees require carbon to build their structures and, along with water and sunlight, provide food. Once the world started to burn coal, oil and gas in huge volumes from the industrial revolution onwards, the amount of emitted carbon dioxide surged at an unprecedented rate, with atmospheric concentrations of CO2 rising by more than 50% in little over a century.
This increase in carbon did initially help boost some plant life, a change that has been seized upon by those who question the facts of climate science. Prominent figures in Donald Trump’s administration have argued that burning fossil fuels is good for the environment.
“CO2 was never a pollutant,” Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, told Fox Business earlier this year as the federal government moved to erase its own power to address the climate crisis. “When we breathe, we emit CO2. Plants need CO2 to survive and grow. They thrive with more CO2.”

England is enduring its fifth heatwave of the summer, with almost three-quarters of the country now in drought but for many Independent readers, the real story isn’t the weather – it’s what’s happening underground.
As hosepipe bans spread to 27 million households, readers have been sharing their own run-ins with the water companies now asking them to cut back: mains leaks left unfixed for years, reservoirs drained while dividends flow abroad, and infrastructure that hasn’t kept pace with the climate crisis. 
Others pointed out that Portugal and France, both hotter and drier this summer, have avoided restrictions altogether by investing in dams and hydro power years ago.





Here’s what you had to say:

Water companies have failed to invest for decades
Water companies have under-invested for decades. Billions have gone abroad in dividends over that time. Still paying out million-pound salaries. We face drought being a more and more common thing with no end to leaks in sight. No major incentives for grey water usage. Swimming pools, golf courses and washing cars are not priorities compared to having water to flush loos, not having water to cook with and to drink.

avidmidlandsreader




A leak reported twice, still not fixed
Where I live, we have had a hosepipe ban for a while now. Today we are officially experiencing a drought. Just outside my house is a water leak that has been reported to the water company at least twice. A symptom of a problem that has been ongoing for at least two years, they “mended” one side of the road, only for it to emerge on the other. It hasn’t flooded the road as all the water runs off into the adjacent canal. It’s shocking that this privatised business makes me restrict my water usage while leaving this leak to waste water, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, week after week!
Umist0966

No living grass within a two-hour drive
I have not mowed my lawns since the 10th of June – normally I’d have cut the grass seven or eight times in the last 60 days. Of 3,000 square metres of grass, only about 20 square metres isn’t dead, and that’s just because it’s shaded by a large tree. There is no living grass anywhere within a two-hour drive of me. I’ve spent my holidays here since 1990 and lived here since 2016 – I’ve never seen a drought like this. The river near here normally makes the Thames look like a brook, but in places I think I could wade across it. Trying to grow onions has been a sick joke; my tomato plants dropped three trusses’ worth of flowers when the temperature didn’t dip below 36C for 14 days running.

Not all swimming pools should be treated the same
Only private pools should be banned, not public pools, which often recycle water by sending it through large filtration plants, often under the pool with the addition of chemicals. ‘Everyone is scared’: flood-hit Porto Alegre braces for another El Niño


Two years after southern Brazil’s worst climate disaster ravaged the city, and with poor areas still recovering, many fear official neglect has left them exposed once again




In the backstreets of Porto Alegre, a state capital in southern Brazil, you can still see signs of the devastating flood that swept through the city two years ago: scattered debris, waterlogged homes and destroyed businesses.
In May 2024, flooding killed 183 people in the state of Rio Grande do Sul and displaced more than 600,000. The neighbourhood of Sarandi was one of the hardest-hit parts of Porto Alegre, with water levels reaching up to 5 metres above normal, completely submerging many of its streets.

“Most people are still suffering the mental health consequences of the flood,” says Luís Rogério “Jamaika” Machado, a community leader in Sarandi.
“They lost absolutely everything. Unable to rebuild their houses, most have become deeply depressed.”


View image in fullscreen
Jamaika at the cultural centre in Quilombo dos Machado. His community provided food, clothing and medical assistance to thousands of families during the 2024 floods
Last month, meteorologists announced the imminent return of El Niño, the naturally occurring phenomenon caused by rising sea-surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific but the effects of which are greatly aggravated by the climate crisis. El Niño, which disrupts weather patterns across the globe, is likely to cause extreme rainfall and flooding in southern Brazil.
Jamaika lives in an urban quilombo, a Brazilian settlement founded by escaped enslaved people or their descendants. Quilombo dos Machado is one of 11 such territories in Porto Alegre and served as a centre of solidarity for the entire Sarandi area during the flood, distributing food, clothing and medical assistance to thousands of families.
Now Porto Alegre’s flood-hit communities, though still recovering from one of Brazil’s deadliest climate disasters, face renewed threats from this year’s developing El Niño as incomplete flood defences and government relocation schemes fuel fears of displacement and deepen a climate justice crisis.


View image in fullscreen
A man walks through the rubble of destroyed homes in Sarandi, Porto Alegre, one of the worst affected nighbourhoods in the 2024 flooding

A late monsoon season earlier this year provided the Great Barrier Reef with a crucial breathing space from coral bleaching, helping the world's largest reef system begin recovering from recent damage.
The rainy conditions boosted cloud cover and brought sea temperatures down, curbing both the severity and spread of bleaching during the 2025/26 summer, according to the Australian Institute of Marine Science's latest annual survey.

 
Findings from the 40th AIMS report reveal that coral cover either grew modestly or held steady across the reef's northern, central and southern zones compared with the previous year.
All three regions maintained coral cover at or close to their long-term averages, suggesting the 2025 mass bleaching event and a regional bleaching episode in early 2026 had only limited effects.

Britons have been urged to keep out of the sun during peak hours as a blistering heatwave brings temperature highs of 37C to the country on Thursday.
The Met Office has issued an amber extreme heat warning for much of England, covering parts of the south and east, as well as swathes of the Midlands.





The warning highlights likely health impacts from the heat, as well as potential water safety incidents, travel disruption and power cuts in some places.
Dr Michael Gregory, regional medical director for NHS England in the North West, urged the public to take precautions and avoid becoming seriously unwell from overheating, dehydration, heat exhaustion or heatstroke.
“Staying out of the sun during the hottest part of the day, from 11am to 3pm, can lower the risk of becoming unwell, he said.


“If you are planning physical activity, such as exercising or walking the dog, try to do this during cooler parts of the day, such as the morning or evening.”
Some rail operators are also urging train passengers to only travel if necessary on Thursday as services will be disrupted because of hot weather.

articles.raw_meta: Only 37 per cent back slowing the EV transition, with younger people and Labour voters keenest to keep things moving, according to new poll
articles.jina_text:
Most people in Britain would rather the government didn’t ease off on the switch to electric cars, according to a new poll arriving as Labour faces fresh questions over its EV plans.
Despite pressure from the car industry for the government to relax the current ZEV mandate that means car makers must hit a 33 per cent target for electric car volume this year, the YouGov survey, commissioned by charging industry trade body ChargeUK, found only 37 per cent believe the move should be slowed. By contrast, 34 per cent think the pace is about right and 19 per cent want it sped up.
That puts 53 per cent in the keep-going-or-go-faster camp, while 11 per cent said they didn’t know.
Among people who voted Labour in 2024, only 21 per cent favour a slowdown. Some 41 per cent are happy with the current pace and 27 per cent want faster progress.





open image in gallery
ChargeUK says that rethinking the ZEV mandate could put charging investment at risk (Vauxhall)
Green voters are keener still, with 30 per cent supporting the current speed and 46 per cent wanting the transition accelerated. Among Liberal Democrat voters, 39 per cent say the pace is right and 25 per cent want it increased.





There’s a clear age split, too. More than a third of 18 to 24-year-olds – 36 per cent – want the transition accelerated. That falls to 21 per cent among 25 to 49-year-olds, 14 per cent for those aged 50 to 64 and 11 per cent among people aged 65 and over.
The findings land as Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s new government comes under pressure over the zero-emission vehicle mandate.

We need urgent reform of the regulation, else Britain risks undermining its competitiveness and the jobs and livelihoods that depend on this industry.”


While car makers have been pushing for changes to the rules, ChargeUK has warned that another rethink could put charging investment at risk.

London, the South East, East of England and East Midlands are set to feel the brunt of the heatwave, with temperatures remaining high for the rest of the week.

Wildfires continue to rip through the landscape in New Forest, Hampshire, and Saddleworth Moor, Oldham.  

 
Firefighters are tackling the blaze in New Forest for a fifth day now after it spread into the precious heathland from a burning van on the A31, which remains shut.  
In Saddleworth, the fire broke out overnight, and people have been asked to avoid the area near Holmfirth today.  
Rail disruption warning 
Several train companies have said they are likely to be hit by disruption due to the weather, and many have told passengers to only travel if essential. 
Extreme heat can cause on-the-ground railway temperatures to top 50°C and rail to buckle. This is why stretches of railway, especially in direct sun, can have speed restrictions in place and fewer trains might be scheduled.  
Chiltern Railways is operating on a reduced timetable between 11am and 8pm as a result to ensure a ‘reliable service’ can be provided ‘during the hottest part of the day’. 
Michael Stewart, from Chiltern Railways, said: ‘If you do need to travel, please check your journey before setting out, allow extra time and carry water with you to stay hydrated.’ 

 
  
He added that customers should travel ‘only if it’s essential on Thursday because of the exceptionally high temperatures forecast across our network’.

Australia’s largest aluminium smelter to run on renewables by 2033 after Rio Tinto strikes $2.5bn taxpayer bailout deal


Rio Tinto makes power supply deal with federal and NSW government to cut emissions and decarbonise, preventing potential closure 
 
 
Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates 
 
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast 




Resources giant Rio Tinto says Australia’s largest aluminium smelter will run entirely on renewable energy by 2033 after it struck a $2.5bn subsidy deal with the federal and New South Wales governments to prevent a potential closure.
The deal – announced by Anthony Albanese and the NSW premier, Chris Minns, at the Tomago smelter near Newcastle on Thursday – is for a 10-year below-market power supply guarantee that begins after the facility’s existing coal-focused electricity contract with AGL ends in December 2028.

The governments said the deal would underpin nearly 3,000 megawatts of new renewable and “firming” capacity in the state, more than a giant coal station.







Australia’s biggest aluminium smelter gets $2.5bn bailout package from federal and NSW governments

Read more
Rio Tinto, a joint owner of the smelter, said it meant by 2033 the smelter would run on clean energy only and cut its annual greenhouse gas emissions by 7.1m tonnes a year, equivalent to 1.5% of Australia’s annual climate pollution.
In a statement, Rio Tinto Aluminium and Lithium’s chief executive, Jérôme Pécresse, said the smelter had a pathway to “long-term, cost-competitive, low-carbon power”.
The deal is the latest in a series of Albanese government bailout packages meant to ensure major industries keep operating. Other commitments include $2bn for Rio Tinto’s Boyne aluminium smelter in Queensland and $2.4bn for steelworks in the South Australian town of Whyalla.

Aluminium production is particularly vulnerable to rising power prices due to its huge electricity use, and the Australian industry has for decades relied on cheap long-term supply deals. Tomago is the country’s largest single electricity user, taking more than 10% of total generation in NSW. It directly employs about 1,000 people, and is claimed to indirectly support about 5,000 more.


The smelter’s owners committed to invest $1.1bn in Tomago over the next 12 years, including $100m for “decarbonisation activities”, as part of the deal.

articles.raw_content:
Firefighters have called for “wildfire-fighting aircraft” to help combat spate of blazes as Britain braces for another heatwave, with temperatures likely to top 35°C.



UK fire brigades do not have direct access to water-bombing planes that can drop up to six tonnes of water onto a blaze, while Britain’s military firefighting helicopters are all deployed in Cyprus.



The Fire Brigades Union (FBU), which represents around 34,000 men and women in the fire and rescue service across the UK, has called for access to aerial firefighting capabilities where “appropriate” to combat a looming risk of larger and more complex wildfires. 





Ministers are understood to be looking closely at which kit is needed now and in the future, including aerial assets, to improve UK capabilities.



But The i Paper understands that the military has not yet been asked to support the Government in tackling the wildfires. 



Any such measure, including the deployment of the RAF’s Chinook firefighting helicopters, would have to come via a “military aid to the civil authorities” request. This has previously been used to deploy troops during the Covid-19 pandemic and the 2021 fuel crisis.



It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired an emergency Cobra meeting on Wednesday afternoon in response to the extreme heat, the second this summer and the first of his premiership.

India fuels worldwide jump in planned coal production 


Rise in new mine proposals, mainly in states of Odisha and Jharkhand, comes despite plateau in global demand




Enough new coalmining projects were proposed last year to increase global supplies by 2.5bn tonnes a year, an increase of 11% from the year before, even as demand for coal plateaus, according to a new report.
Global Energy Monitor, an NGO, found that India ignited a rise in new coalmine proposals in 2025 despite a global slowdown in the number of mine openings because of falling demand for the fossil fuel.

The increase was driven almost entirely by the states of Jharkhand and Odisha, which doubled their proposals for new coalmines in line with an ambitious plan from India’s ministry of coal to increase the country’s output.






The Guardian view on India’s green growth gamble: it will need more than private finance

Read more
India plans to increase its coal production by nearly 100m tonnes to 1.15bn tonnes in the 2025-26 fiscal year to help meet the country’s rising demand for electricity to support economic growth and contend with heatwaves, which have become more severe and more frequent because of the climate crisis.
The planned increases come despite signs that the world is beginning to turn its back on coal in favour of renewable electricity, Global Energy Monitor said.


Coalmine proposals slowed in the years after the Covid-19 pandemic but have begun to climb again, raising concerns that mining could increase in the future despite a slowdown in the number of new facilities.
The startup of new coalmining projects has fallen steadily in recent years, according to the Global Energy Monitor’s latest report.
It found that enough new coalmines to produce about 113m tonnes each year began operations last year, down by 40% from 2024, which was already the lowest annual total in a decade.
This was largely owing to a slowdown in new mines in China and Australia, which fell by 44% and 96% respectively.
Global Energy Monitor warned that India’s rise in new mine proposals was at odds with the slowdown in global coal demand predicted by the International Energy Agency for the end of the decade.

Potatoes ‘boil’ in the ground as record heatwave sweeps across swathes of Asia


South Korean farmers are suffering in record heat, as Hong Kong reports its highest ever temperature and Japan swelters through newly designated ‘cruelly hot’ days




In a potato field in Yanggu county, 80 miles (130km) north-east of Seoul, Lee Sang-hyuk dug into the soil and found nothing worth saving.
A week earlier the crop, located in Gangwon province, had looked fine. Now the potatoes came up soft and collapsing, “like boiled potatoes”, spoiled by heat that had turned the ground into something closer to an oven.

“It’s not just one or two fields like this. How can I even put it into words? It’s so upsetting,” he told local broadcaster SBS.
His ruined harvest is one thread in a punishing summer across east Asia, as record heat swept through South Korea, Japan and Hong Kong in recent weeks.

On 2 August, the south-eastern city of Yangsan recorded a temperature of 42.5C, the highest registered in South Korea since modern weather observations began in 1904.


The heat has since been blamed for at least 31 deaths nationwide, according to the country’s disease control agency, while more than 900,000 livestock and 1.4 million farmed fish have died.
Authorities issued a heat warning, urging people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”.
South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, told his cabinet the extreme weather was “unlike anything we have experienced before”.
“We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system,” he said, “since this extreme weather is becoming the new normal.”

In Tokyo, three lions died of suspected heatstroke at a city zoo.

Three-quarters of England is now officially in drought. Firefighters are continuing to tackle a blaze in the New Forest in Hampshire, with warnings across parts of eastern and southern Scotland about a very high risk of wildfires.

On Tuesday, Kim Doster, the communications director of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), said the federal agency was withdrawing its support for the Arctic Report Card, which has provided environmental updates on the region to scientists and the public since 2006.

Without explaining why the government stopped its support, Doster told the New York Times: “Coordination of the 2026 Arctic Report Card will not be facilitated through NOAA … All data historically contributed by NOAA to the product will continue to be collected and will remain publicly available.”
Doster told the outlet that other Noaa programs would continue to support research in the region that contributes to “national security, weather prediction, safety of navigation and the economic vitality of coastal communities”.

The climate crisis has made the Arctic the world’s fastest-warming region. In recent years, the region has experienced severe sea ice decline, carbon sink reversals and ecosystem upheavals.
In the 2025 Arctic Report Card, scientists found that surface temperatures across the Arctic from October 2024 through September 2025 were the warmest recorded since 1900. It also found that in March 2025, Arctic winter sea ice reached the lowest annual maximum extent in the 47-year satellite record.


Meanwhile, on land, the report noted that ongoing glacier loss contributes to steadily rising global sea levels, threatening Arctic communities’ water supplies, driving destructive floods, and increasing landslide and tsunami hazards.

View image in fullscreen
The solar eclipse is expected to wipe out solar power generation, so Neso may make payments to energy generators to help fill the gap Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images


Great Britain braced to pay millions for backup electricity during solar eclipse


Event expected to curtail solar power just as summer’s fifth heatwave increases use of air conditioning and fans




Great Britain is braced to pay millions for backup electricity supplies to prevent a shortfall on Wednesday evening as the near-total solar eclipse is expected to wipe out solar power generation.
The government’s electricity grid operator is expected to make multimillion-pound payments to secure electricity at short notice before the moon blocks up to 95% of the sun over parts of the country, the most dramatic solar eclipse visible in Great Britain since 1999.

Gas plants are among the generators that are expected to claim payments of more than four times the market price after the grid operator raised an official alarm that it expects there will not be adequate power generation on Wednesday evening.







Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipse

Read more
The Connah’s Quay gas plant in Flintshire, owned by the German utility company Uniper, agreed to generate electricity on Wednesday afternoon for a price of £875 per megawatt-hour, compared with the market price of just below £212/MWh for this evening.
The payment suggests that the gas plant may be kept running through the evening to help meet the rising demand for electricity, possibly at even higher prices. The darkening of the skies is expected to wipe out between 300 megawatts (MW) and 1,100MW of solar power, just as the fifth heatwave of the summer raises demand for electricity to run air conditioning, fans and refrigeration systems.
The National Energy System Operator (Neso) had initially anticipated an overall shortfall of more than 1,700MW of electricity when compared with the grid’s peak evening demand, according to a warning issued on Tuesday night, or the equivalent capacity of a solar farm the size of 8,500 football pitches.


Under a second market notice issued on Wednesday morning, it said the shortfall remained about 1,200MW.
A spokesperson described the warning notice as a “routine tool” that meant it was asking the energy market to make any additional capacity the generators might have available.
It added that the margin notice was a “precautionary measure to the market” because of the solar eclipse and there was “no risk to customer electricity supplies”.

From grey water to cool spaces: 10 climate crisis policies Britain needs right now


Rejecting North Sea drilling licences and protecting nature are just some measures Andy Burnham must implement to ready country




From record-smashing temperatures, wildfires, hosepipe bans and thousands of premature deaths, the climate crisis has left its mark across the summer of 2026.
Tackling the root cause – the burning of fossil fuels – and ending the crisis will take years. So will fixing the UK government’s calamitous failure to protect lives and livelihoods against the long-predicted affects of global heating.

But the climate emergency is right here, right now, and here are 10 policies that Andy Burnham’s government should consider announcing urgently.
1. Reject drilling licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gasfields
This would be a vital and confidence-boosting sign that the UK is committed to putting a rocket-booster under the clean, green and very fast-growing economy of the 21st century, not the fossil-fuelled one of the last. It would also give diplomatic weight to the UK as it works internationally to cut emissions and end the climate crisis.
The supposed benefits of approving the North Sea oil and gasfields are mostly fantasy. They will have no impact on UK energy prices – oil and gas are commodities whose price is set by international markets. As the UK Energy Research Council says: “Assertions that drilling the North Sea will provide energy resilience and affordability in the face of current fuel price shocks are a delusion.”
As for jobs, the licences would support very few – again, unlike the growing green economy. Some also argue North Sea production is less carbon intensive than imports, but that ignores the far cleaner record of our main gas importer, Norway, as well as the methane emissions from LNG, and in any case the differences are small compared with CO2 savings of using renewable energy and storage instead of gas.
2. Increase windfall tax on fossil fuel giants to pay for adaptation measures
When people say money is tight, remember the eight biggest oil companies made a staggering $93bn in the three months to the end of June – almost double their profits from the same period last year. At the same time, carbon emissions from the oil and gas these companies produce are driving the escalating climate crisis, and bills for ordinary consumers continue to rise. An increased windfall tax on these excess profits could raise huge sums for government coffers and help pay for emergency adaptation measures.

articles.jina_text:
My child and I were bonding over our hit-and-miss approach to reaping crops. But with heatwaves pushing more of Britain into drought, it’s starting to feel like a luxury we can’t afford





For the first time in my life, I live in a home that has real outdoor space. What a concept! There are no downsides to a garden. Back in spring, I made grand plans – I watched all the TikToks, I bought seeds and trays and pots and grow bags, I ordered soil, a trowel and a watering can. I knew what I was after: super-tiny-scale subsistence farming with a side of Zen. A little fruit, a little veg, lots of flowers to attract pollinators. And I knew I wanted my elder child to gain an understanding of how things come to be and how to cope if and when they fail.
We love a tomato side salad, so that was the first thing we attempted. The seedlings flourished and then died in the first heatwave of the season. An omen, surely. The dahlias, ranunculus and freesias refused to grow, let alone bloom. My enthusiasm began to wane.



But then: our first harvest! Three (three!) bright-red Tumbling Tom tomatoes. We halved them, then tossed them in olive oil with some salt and pepper. They were gone in the blink of an eye, but we were grinning as we chomped. Ah, the pleasure of growing something small you can eat. We have sown onions, carrots, lettuce and basil and eagerly await miniature crops as the days get shorter.
At the back of my mind, though, is the very real fear of food shortages. Britain is approaching its sixth climate-crisis-induced heatwave of the year. Drought no longer threatens the country – it’s here. Conflicts around the world have inflated food prices. Is everyone aware of this? And are they in a state of low-grade panic, too?
What was supposed to feel like a fun bonding experience with my kid is morphing into something darker. Our garden has been heavy on trial and error, which feels increasingly like a luxury. Fun over – time to get good at this, fast. I know I’m doing too much, but I’ve started considering Kilner jars at TK Maxx and following homesteaders who grow their own produce. My favourite doomscroll these days is planting calendars and seed catalogues. Send tips, please. See you at the garden centre.
 Bim Adewunmi is a freelance journalist

Actually, though, that £1bn bill stems not from the fact wind power is bad but because it’s too good. According to The Times, “most of the cost comes from paying gas-fired power plants to fire up to cover for wind turbines that have to be turned off because of” – here comes the kicker – “insufficient cabling capacity”. As more wind power has come on stream, more capacity to transport it to actual people hasn’t. That, thanks to Britain’s esoteric energy market, means we’re now paying renewable energy suppliers in rural areas to switch off (so as not to overload the network), and fossil fuels nearer actual people to switch on (because we still need the power). And the more turbines we have, the more that bill will go up. Oops. 
These figures come from the Wasted Wind website supported by Octopus Energy, which is currently lobbying the government to end this madness by replacing national energy pricing with a more regional scheme. For those without such skin in the game, though, this mess provides proof of a much simpler thesis: that Britain has lost the ability to build the infrastructure it needs to function.

 
When you go looking for evidence for this problem, you start seeing it everywhere (or rather, you don’t, because nobody’s built it). The largest, most expensive and highest profile mess is HS2, which as originally conceived would have connected almost every major British city and, by adding capacity and removing bottlenecks, benefited smaller places far off the route, too. 
After spiralling costs and repeated cutbacks, alas, it will instead serve mainly to create a third mainline route between London and Birmingham and not a lot else. The reasons for this have more to do with political chaos and over-scoping in a doomed attempt to assuage Nimbys than with the project itself, but nonetheless, this is not a lot to show for a bill of £100bn+. It’s all a little embarrassing for the nation that invented the railways. 

London’s Hammersmith Bridge closed to motor traffic due to structural problems in 2019 (Photo: Richard Baker/Getty)

That, thanks to Britain’s esoteric energy market, means we’re now paying renewable energy suppliers in rural areas to switch off (so as not to overload the network), and fossil fuels nearer actual people to switch on (because we still need the power). And the more turbines we have, the more that bill will go up. Oops.



These figures come from the Wasted Wind website supported by Octopus Energy, which is currently lobbying the government to end this madness by replacing national energy pricing with a more regional scheme. For those without such skin in the game, though, this mess provides proof of a much simpler thesis: that Britai
articles.summary: Britain has spent £1bn this year paying wind farms to switch off due to insufficient grid cabling capacity, while simultaneously paying gas-fired power plants to compensate for the lost power. The problem stems not from wind power being ineffective, but from a failure to build the transmission infrastructure needed to transport renewable energy to consumers. The article uses this as an example of a broader pattern of the UK failing to build necessary infrastructure, also citing the repeated cutbacks to HS2.

All-British chocolate bar made by scientists using Reading-grown cocoa


Master’s student made first bar with 100% UK ingredients since 1932 to highlight effect of climate crisis on cocoa plants




The late queen was the only person in history to have ever eaten a chocolate bar made with 100% British ingredients, after she was given one as a six-year-old in 1932 by the confectioner Rowntree’s.
The bar was created from a glasshouse-grown cocoa plant, at Rowntree’s headquarters in York.

But now, others could have the same experience after scientists at the University of Reading created a bar with cocoa beans grown in Berkshire.


Raw cacao beans are coated in a white flesh ‘that tastes like lychee’. Photograph: University of Reading
The bar was crafted to celebrate the university’s 100th anniversary, made with cocoa grown from plants in the institute’s collection.


The UK makes some of the world’s best chocolate in a market worth £10.4bn, but the industry is entirely reliant on imported cocoa.
Maha Khan, a master’s student at the university, decided to make a bar with cocoa from Reading. She harvested, fermented, and processed the beans at the university’s food department.







Why hot weather and chocolate can go together

Read more
She said: “It has been amazing to follow the entire chocolate-making process, from pod to bean to bar, without leaving Reading.
“This British bar of chocolate highlights the precarious nature of our food supplies. Cocoa plants are very sensitive to changes in temperature and rainfall, and climate change is already causing problems in countries that produce most of the world’s cocoa. Protecting different varieties is vital if farmers need hardier plants that can cope with a changing climate.
“I hope this shows people just how much work goes into the chocolate we enjoy, and how important it is to protect cocoa farmers and communities around the world.”
She said the chocolate is “delicious”, adding that it had a very rich flavour: “It’s incredible to taste the complexity of the flavour profiles as the cocoa is made from plants originating from over 300 varieties grown here. It was also really interesting to taste the raw cacao before it gets processed – the beans are coated in a white flesh that tastes like lychee and isn’t something many people in this country get to try.”

articles.raw_rss: It is understood ministers will launch a consultation in the coming days on loosening net-zero rules for sales of electric vehicles
articles.raw_content:
Consumers could see an end to “heavy” discounts on electric vehicles (EVs) as ministers look to water down net-zero targets, according to car industry experts.



Under current laws, 80 per cent of all new cars sold in the UK must be electric by 2030 under the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, rising from 33 per cent from 2026. 



It is understood that ministers are set to launch a consultation in the coming days on loosening these rules, with numbers ranging from 50 per cent to 70 per cent under consideration. 





The European Commission has already modified its plans to ban the sale of petrol and diesel vehicles by 2035, shifting the requirement for a 100 per cent ban on internal combustion engines to a 90 per cent zero-emissions target.



Good deals on electric cars



The Department for Transport (DfT) said it is “committed” to phasing out new petrol and diesel cars from 2030 but said it would “review the mandate to support British industry and investment”, with further details to be published in due course.



It comes after intense lobbying from car manufacturers who argue the mandate is too strict and leads to huge, last-minute discounts on EVs as they attempt to hit their quotas to avoid fines of £12,000 for every non-compliant vehicle sold.

articles.raw_rss: Climate change and El Niño are working together to make your summer extra hot
articles.raw_meta: Climate change and El Niño are working together to make your summer extra hot
articles.jina_text:
July was just the hottest month on record in the contiguous U.S., according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration - and shows little signs of slowing down for August. 
Fortunately, it appears temperatures will drop for many areas this week - but much of the southern U.S. will see dangerous heat before the end of August.
“Potentially record-breaking heat will grip the Southeast to south-central U.S. into next week, with heat indices reaching 105–115 degrees Fahrenheit and little nighttime relief,” NOAA’s National Weather Service warned. 





August is typically not quite as hot as July, but meteorologists say the record sets up August for more extreme events. Some local records have already been broken. 
“Wow - Pueblo just set its all-time hottest August temperature on record. 107 degrees at the Pueblo Airport so far,” Colorado meteorologist Chris Bianchi wrote on Bluesky. “That's also just two degrees shy of the all-time hottest temp there.”

The Guardian view on wildfires: firefighters can’t handle this crisis alone

Editorial





The response to this summer’s record heat and drought should be led by ministers – not left to the emergency services





The wildfire that began on protected heathland in the New Forest in Hampshire on Sunday was reported to be under control on Tuesday. But with temperatures forecast to reach 36C or higher in parts of England on Thursday, the risk of further outbreaks remains high. Firefighters responded to 185 wildfires in the first 10 days of August. In coastal Suffolk, conservationists and locals are counting the cost of the blaze that devastated Dunwich Heath. Its vegetation and rare bird populations are expected to take decades to recover.
Although the immediate cause of many wildfires is litter, the risks are elevated by heat and drought, and repeated warnings from climate scientists do not necessarily lessen the shock and distress caused. As people and governments across Europe assess this summer’s damage, experts including the UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, hope that the fires will focus minds on the urgent necessity of cutting emissions – as well as investing in emergency planning. Europe is currently heating up faster than any other continent, due in part to proximity to the melting Arctic.



The global, existential nature of the climate crisis makes it an awkward fit with Andy Burnham’s current focus on “everyday fixes”. But if he does not find more to say about the summer’s disasters, he is in danger of being left behind. The National Trust has already surpassed its £500,000 fundraising target to restore Dunwich Heath. Conservationists and farmers are publicly debating the best ways to prevent fires. The Fire Brigades Union (FBU) is pushing for 5,000 additional firefighters across the UK, along with new equipment.


View image in fullscreen
Hilary McGrady, the National Trust director general. Photograph: Shutterstock
In March, the then fire safety minister, Samantha Dixon, said that the fire and rescue service had suffered from “decades of drift and inertia”. Her speech also confirmed that a new College of Fire and Rescue would oversee professional standards, as recommended by the Grenfell inquiry. But three weeks ago Ms Dixon was sacked. If the government wants to avoid an impression that drift and inertia are ongoing, they need to provide an update, along with a response to repeated calls from the fire service inspectorate for new enforcement powers. MPs on the home affairs committee threw their weight behind this idea two years ago.

Exclusive satellite imagery prepared by geospatial analytics company Map Impact for The Standard shows how the capital’s parks, gardens and other green oases are being frazzled into parched lands.




Normally, London is one of the greenest capitals on earth, boasting “crown jewel” parks like no other city.











But across the drought-hit capital of nine million, the landscape has been ravaged by the relentless baking heat with temperatures forecast to hit 35C on Thursday in London.




The images from space lay bare the impact of virtually no rain for weeks and record temperatures, no more so than in Victoria Park, in Tower Hamlets, the capital’s oldest public park.


Victoria Park

Its normally lush, green acres are now vast, straw-coloured areas.




The dramatic transformation has happened in just months.




The satellite snaps show how the park looked in March - before the global warming-fuelled extraordinary heat hit Britain - and then in July. 




The “People’s Park”, as it has been known over the years, was opened in 1845 for the benefit of the East End working class, and sprawls across 86 hectares as part of a “green corridor” in the capital.




But the park, visited by more than nine million people a year, is now far from green.




Its remaining grass and other vegetation is set to further wilt in the “extreme” heat forecast to peak on Thursday.

Even St James’s Park and Green Park, around Buckingham Palace, have been turned into “tinderboxes”.




Amid the high temperatures, the threat of wildfires has spiralled so significantly that Sir Sadiq Khan has urged Londoners to create fire breaks in their own gardens to protect their homes.
